The machine can not record single direction’s movements and it can only save the movements within 30mm ,the move distance was  deponds on the fixing plate ,So the real movement is actually a data of the maximum value（pull direction） minus the minimum value （push direction),just like this : the movement for the push is 33.9mm -the movement for the pull is 29.5mm =4.4mm ,it is the both direction movement not for the single direction

What was the reason of the issue?
1. We create a integration system. 
[https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/delivery/automation/delivery_automation/main/service/AutomationService.ts#L317|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/delivery/automation/delivery_automation/main/service/AutomationService.ts#L317] 
[https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/delivery/automation/delivery_automation/main/adapter/ProviderPOSAdapter.ts#L28|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/delivery/automation/delivery_automation/main/adapter/ProviderPOSAdapter.ts#L28] 
As a result, a new integration system is added to a primary db
2. We try to create a provider integration with just received integration system id
3. While creating a provider integration *delivery-provider-pos* queries integration system by id from secondary db
4. Sometimes newly created integration system is not replicated to the secondary db yet.

An update on the comms coverage numbers based on the updated targeting definition of {{only considering the comms that were sent while the user was in a particular stage}}.

*Overall Comms Coverage Numbers*
At an overall level, the activation stage has seen the maximum decline of 10% compared to the old definition for addressable users receiving stage relevant + other comms. This gap is arising because of cases in which a user saw a change in lifecycle stage during the observation period (including activation). We would need to understand what comms these users are receiving.

*Comms Coverage By Tenure*
While discussing the numbers with the Driver team, I noticed that there was a slight difference in the way tenure is interpreted across Driver and Rider. For example, if a user belonged to the activation stage before April and stayed there into April (e.g., Feb 1 to April 10), and then moved to churn, it was labeled as "new-entry" for Rider and "carry-over" for Driver. After discussing with the Driver team, we now label such cases as "carry-over" to keep definitions consistent across verticals.This difference mainly affects the activation stage as the distribution of users between new-entry and carry-over has changed the most in this lifecycle stage.After applying the new targeting definition to the data split by lifecycle stage and tenure, we see that the coverage numbers have declined for all instances, which is to be expected as the new definition is more precise in targeting.The [Google Sheet|https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1wZerZOI3Bkr7qJnWKd8rm_rkzK7dUgIr0jCvOV9-cEo/edit?gid=2135018459#gid=2135018459] has been updated with the latest numbers.

*Update 21.07.2025*

*Incrementality tests* [https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/MARTECH3-93|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/MARTECH3-93|smart-link]

* *Results*
At the Step 2 level, there’s no evidence of incrementality seen in all piloted markets (UA, KE and GH). Apart from actual non-incrementality, there are a few other hypotheses that could lead to the same result:
** Current methodology is not sensitive enough to detect small changes (especially since only a handful of drivers make referrals
** Referral program does not materially impact overall lead volume, but may be impactful at the activation level (which incrementality’s is currently not measured ). In UA and KE, attributed referral leads are ~2x more likely to convert from Step 2 Leads to Activations (30-day Window). Interestingly, this is not true for Accra, GH as the activation rate for referral leads is pretty much the same as non-referrals - given the prevalence of fraud in the market, it may be indeed the case that driver referral is really not incremental in this market.
** Unaccounted third variable that could neutralise the effect (e.g. in the case of Accra where model is detecting an uplift rather than the expected drop from the blackout test in the city). Note that acquisition ad spend was stable throughout the measurement period.
** Note that while we were not able to detect incrementality in the three pilot markets, such results are not uncommon; similar geo experiment design in online ads yield ~40% of success (i.e. incrementality detected at >90% confidence). We expect improved sensitivity in our measurements as we further refine the methodology.
* *Next Steps (Q3)*
** Retry measurements in UA and KE using cohorted activations i.e. activation dated to signup date as the test metric (NB these are not new experiments).
** Research on city-level experiment design repeat UA experiment with such design (if feasible)
* *To Consider in Backlog*
** Repeat experiment in KE as a blackout test instead
** Plan for next round of incrementality experiments, ideally at the city-level. Possible candidates for other markets: PY, RO, FR

Hi [~accountid:63985ce2f7f0ee492fcea284] 

Replying to the customer questions:

# *Service Fee*

Answer: this is a business question. Emin, you need to obtain an approval from your manager. If they agree,  then we should also cap this and suggest introducing the reevaluation, for instance, every 3 months. Let me know if you get an approval and then we can think how to word this clause.

# *Late Payment and Compensation for Expenses*

Answer: While we understand the desire to limit financial exposure, we can't accept a fixed cap — actual recovery costs (especially legal or third-party collections) often exceed suggested cap. Similarly, pre-agreed grace periods weaken enforcement predictability and could invite repeated delays. 

To clarify, our clause is not intended to punish. The 5% annual interest is modest and aligned with commercial norms — it's there to discourage repeated late payments. As long as there’s cooperation, we’re always open to flexible arrangements. But if there’s no payment and no communication, it’s both reasonable and standard for Bolt to escalate and seek cost reimbursement. This clause simply protects us in those rare but serious cases.

# *Priority of Language*

Answer: We can simply delete the clause from the Special Terms because the General Terms already have clause 8.9 - _In case of conflict between the English and the Azerbaijani text, the English text shall prevail._ 

# Credit or refund for undelivered services

Answer: It's important to note that Bolt Services are provided on an “as is” and “as available” basis. This means we do not — and cannot — guarantee that a driver will always accept or complete a ride. Cancellations may occur for reasons outside Bolt’s control, such as driver decisions or user no-shows.

Our platform is already designed to not charge for undelivered services in most such cases — and we do issue credits where appropriate, especially if there’s a fault on our side.



Have a sunny day and let me know if you have any questions.

I just had a look at the Service Terms that you sent.

I've reviewed the Supplier Agreement from the third party. This agreement does not pass review as several terms breach our guidelines.

*Key Terms*

* Term: Indefinite
* Termination Notice Period: Not specified
* Governing Law: Republic of Estonia
* Jurisdiction: Harju County Court
* Indemnity: No

*Non-compliant provisions:*

*1 - Warranties*
The document lacks explicit supplier warranties covering legal compliance, service quality, and the use of qualified personnel as required by the playbook.

*2 - Compliance with Law*
The document omits a clause requiring the Supplier to comply with all applicable laws and to notify Bolt of any legal changes impacting the services.

*3 - Confidentiality*
The confidentiality clause does not specify that its obligations survive termination nor does it mandate the return or secure destruction of confidential information.

*4 - Publicity*
The document breaches the Publicity guideline by lacking any clause that restricts the Supplier from issuing publicity or using Bolt's name/logo without prior written consent.

*5 - Intellectual Property Rights*
The document breaches the Intellectual Property Rights guideline by omitting provisions that ensure Bolt owns all bespoke IPR and secures necessary licenses for any supplier IPR used in deliverables.

*6 - Audit Rights*
The document breaches the Audit Rights guideline by not including a provision that permits Bolt to conduct audits to verify compliance with the Agreement.

*7 - Limitation of Liability*
The document lacks a proper Limitation of Liability clause that caps liabilities and clearly lists exclusions for indirect or consequential losses as required.

*8 - Change of Control*
The agreement does not include a Change of Control clause that allows Bolt to terminate if the Supplier undergoes a change in ownership.

*9 - Termination for Cause*
The termination provisions are inadequate, as the document fails to specify detailed conditions for termination for cause such as material breach with cure periods, failure to meet performance milestones, or insolvency events.

*10 - Termination Convenience*
The contract lacks a termination for convenience clause in the termination provisions.

*11 - Consequences of Termination*
The contract does not clearly outline post-termination obligations regarding data, support, or surviving provisions.

*12 - Subcontracting*
The contract does not include any clause that restricts subcontracting without Bolt's prior written consent.

*13 - Force Majeure*
The Force Majeure clause does not expressly grant Bolt the right to suspend payment and engage third parties.

*14 - Dispute Resolution*
The dispute resolution process is not structured as required, lacking mediation and an arbitration option.

*15 - Governing Law and Jurisdiction or Arbitration*
The contract lacks an explicit arbitration option and a clearly defined governing law clause that meets Bolt's requirements.

Thanks,
Supplier Agreements Agent

*Breakdown is not mandatory, but total price is.* According to the law, the total price must be clear before the transaction, including all taxes and additional charges.

* There is no obligation to show how the total is calculated (e.g., €/km or €/min), unless misleading or unfair practices are suspected.
* *Additional charges must be explicit.* For example Airport fees, tolls, or parking fees must be disclosed *clearly and separately*, either *in-app before booking or at the point of confirmation*. 
* F*or the unforeseen costs* - our Terms and Conditions already state that unforeseen costs may be added and that the initial price shown is subject to change. However, any such additional costs must be clearly displayed to the rider at the end of the ride

Let me know if this answers your questions.

Please review the draft and my comments below. I also left some comments in the document.

* Repayment of the Financial Support (500k provided by Bolt) - in your conditions you often mention that “tranches” of the payment can be stopped in certain circumstances, but this contradicts the statement that the sum should be paid in a single transfer. This is good and bad at the same time: this is good, because it allows Bolt to interpret them wider in case of an issue. This is bad because if we end up in court some of the provisions may not be enforceable due to them being too vague. 
* Some tactics and conditions mentioned by you pose risk from competition perspective (depending on what is Bolt’s market share):
** *SKU Exclusivity & Non-Promo Enforcement*: this could be a problem if they significantly restrict the Partner’s ability to offer promotions elsewhere, potentially reducing competition. Make sure that the exclusivity does not extend beyond what is necessary to protect Bolt’s interests. Limiting exclusivity to short, well-defined periods (e.g., Hero Weekends or Full Exclusive Days) may help mitigate concerns. Providing flexibility or opting for a "soft" exclusivity (e.g., geographic or time-limited) may also reduce competition law risks.
** *Competitive Promo Ceilings & Menu Segmentation*: setting specific ceilings for discount offerings on competing platforms can potentially be seen as price-fixing, a practice prohibited under competition laws. In the current draft there is no real ceiling on the discounts, just the requirement for discounts to be the same, but still keep this in mind.
* We say that Dristor should invest “An average of 15% of monthly GMV.” for the marketing campaigns, but we don’t say how often they should invest. Also at least monthly?
* We say that in case of insolvency and liquidation we may demand the repayment of the Financial Support. Please keep in mind that in case these event will take place it is unlikely that the Partner will have the money to repay us anything.

I've been looking for a case like this. We’ve charged the user twice for the scooter pass. This can happen when a user purchases a pass and places a rental order within a very short timespan (less than one minute). The scooter pass payment takes some time to settle, and if it hasn’t settled yet, the user’s Bolt balance becomes negative.

As a result, the user is prompted to pay off their negative balance during the rental order, which leads to a double charge. Once the pass payment settles, the funds are returned to the user's Bolt balance.

We fixed 98% of these cases back in May, but it looks like this user is still affected.

I’ll follow up with the Commerce Engineers and will provide an update as soon as I hear back from them.

----

 Monsieur Djerbi,

Nous accusons réception de vos messages des 13 et 14 juillet 2025 concernant votre statut d’indépendant, le traitement de votre taux d’annulation et les conditions de rémunération liées aux courses annulées par les clients. Nous vous remercions pour votre franchise et souhaitons, par la présente, vous apporter une réponse juridique complète et transparente.

h4. 1. Concernant *votre statut d’indépendant*

Nous vous confirmons que vous intervenez en tant que prestataire de services indépendant, conformément au cadre contractuel qui vous lie à Bolt.

Les Conditions Générales d’Utilisation applicables depuis le 15 juillet 2025 stipulent expressément (article 10.4) :

{quote}_« [...] la relation entre les parties ne constitue pas un contrat de travail, et ne crée aucun lien de subordination entre le Prestataire et Bolt. »_{quote}

Vous conservez une pleine liberté dans l’organisation de votre activité, notamment en ce qui concerne vos horaires et la sélection des courses. Cela est confirmé à l’article 4.6 :

{quote}_« Le Chauffeur a la possibilité d'accepter, de refuser ou d'ignorer des demandes de Clients [...] à sa convenance et sans conséquence sur le maintien du présent Contrat. »_{quote}

Bolt agit uniquement en tant que plateforme technique de mise en relation et ne fournit pas les services de transport eux-mêmes (article 10.3).

h4. 2. *Concernant le taux d’annulation*

Le suivi de certaines données d’activité, comme le taux d’annulation, n’a pas vocation à restreindre votre indépendance. En revanche, comme tout service d’intermédiation numérique, Bolt se doit d’assurer une qualité et une continuité de service pour l’ensemble des utilisateurs.

Certaines pratiques sont donc encadrées lorsqu’elles portent atteinte au bon fonctionnement de la plateforme. L’article 11.3.1 interdit, par exemple, les *annulations excessives après acceptation d’une course*, non pas pour limiter vos refus, mais pour prévenir des comportements désorganisant la mise en relation :

{quote}_« [...] en annulant de manière excessive des services de transport à la demande après avoir indiqué votre volonté de les fournir. »_{quote}

Ce dispositif est prévu par le *règlement européen (UE) 2022/2065 dit « Digital Services Act (DSA)*, qui impose aux plateformes en ligne comme Bolt de mettre en place des règles transparentes, non discriminatoires et proportionnées afin de garantir un fonctionnement équitable. Cela implique que toute mesure d’équilibrage (comme la gestion des taux d’annulation) doit reposer sur des critères *objectifs*, *accessibles*, et *contestables*.

Nous nous conformons à ces exigences et vous pouvez, si besoin, faire valoir vos observations via notre [Système Interne de Traitement des Plaintes|https://bolt.eu/fr-fr/legal/tnc-internal-rules/?category=rides], prévu à l’article 14.6.

h4. 3. *Sur la rémunération en cas d’annulation par un client*

Lorsque le client annule une course au-delà du délai prévu dans l’application, vous pouvez bénéficier d’une compensation (article 4.14) :

{quote}_« [...] le Prestataire a droit à une partie du Prix pour les Services de transport annulés (tel que communiqué au Chauffeur). »_{quote}

Nous vous rappelons que l'application indique, à chaque annulation, si des frais sont dus. Si vous estimez qu’une indemnité n’a pas été appliquée à tort, vous pouvez soumettre une demande via l’outil de révision du prix, dans un délai de 24 heures (article 4.13).

Enfin, nous vous prions de noter que Bolt respecte strictement vos droits en tant que travailleur indépendant et s’efforce d’appliquer un cadre équilibré, conforme aux exigences du droit français et européen. Si vous souhaitez faire valoir certains éléments ou demander des ajustements, nous vous invitons à utiliser le système prévu à cet effet, accessible [ici|https://bolt.eu/fr-fr/legal/tnc-internal-rules/?category=rides].

Nous vous remercions pour votre engagement sur la plateforme et restons à votre disposition pour toute clarification complémentaire.

Veuillez recevoir, Monsieur, nos salutations distinguées.

h3. *How Metrics Are Made*

We use two key *dimensions* to build and filter these metrics:

# *Offer Status*: Reflects the lifecycle stage (Created, Sent, Accepted, Rejected).
# *Latest Offer Status*: Captures the final outcome (accepted, rejected, deprecated, unresolved).

h3. *Key Offer Metrics & Definitions*

* *Offer Sent*: Number of offers that were formally sent, where latest status is not “*deprecated*.”
→ *June 2025 value: 65*
* *Offer Accepted*: Offers where the latest offer status is “accepted.”
→ *June 2025 value: 119*
* *Offer Rejected*: Offers where the latest offer status is “rejected.”
→ *June 2025 value: 37*
* *Offer Acceptance Rate*:
{{Offer Accepted / (Offer Accepted + Offer Rejected)}}
→ *June 2025 value: 76.3%*

Hello [~accountid:712020:08485d64-da8c-4826-8ee4-512427d52ff5]. I do not agree that is the appropriate response. 

Law enforcement requests in PT are not compatible with this standardized approach, where we always ask for the legal basis and the letterhead document.

Repeatedly responding this could actually damage Bolt’s relationship with Police authorities and, in this particular case, I don’t believe it will produce any practical result, since the Police will most likely not comply with this request, since they legally are legitimized to request such information.

Considering that the authority did not specify any deadlines, the default deadline is considered to be 10 days.

IMO, it is best not to ask the Police for the legal basis and the letterhead document, and only respond when we have concrete information to provide or a concrete legal reason to refute providing such information (depending on wether we decide to respond or to seek external legal counsel).

*Quick status update re/ AKI INQUIRY-2977-7 related to login vulnerability breach* *:*

* This is the second time AKI has questioned our Article 34 assessment (the first time was 2977-5 in March 2025 [here|https://drive.google.com/drive/u/0/folders/1qdPahqfn5MSDFbQam1dRGORyhhZMdUhD]) and *_disagreed with the decision to notify only those individuals who experienced financial loss._*
** *_AKI suggests that all affected individuals should be notified (again)_*, arguing that an attacker may still have access to the leaked data and could potentially use it for fraudulent purposes.
* Given this repeated feedback, it’s clear that AKI is taking a conservative stance. If we choose not to notify all affected individuals after the second ask from AKI, *_we might risk enforcement action unless we have a strong and defensible position_*_._
** At the same time, I’m hesitant to set a precedent of notifying individuals in cases where no sensitive data (incl. IDs) was exposed and no material harm was observed (the individuals we did not notify had not suffered any financial loss or any other proved harm).
** Therefore, accepting this logic now could make it more difficult to justify a different position in future since confidentiality risk, to some extent, will always exist.

*Suggested approach:*

* I will have a call with Infosec tomorrow to assess whether the leaked data from rider's and bolt food accounts could realistically be used for known cyberattacks or misused in any other way. If Infosec confirms that such likelihood is low because of for example additional data or steps required, we can push back on the notification recommendation this time one more time, supported by a concrete risk analysis from Infosec.
* If Infosec is unable to provide strong arguments that the risk of misuse is low, we can reassess and consider next steps.

[~accountid:5fd3451c208dbf0107a517db]  Thanks so much for highlighting these points, and my sincere apologies for the oversight. I completely understand your frustration, there’s been a lot happening in parallel, but I take full responsibility. I’ll make sure to be more attentive moving forward.🙏 

Let’s start with the supply side and go through this case by case, as it’s not straightforward and somewhat complex.

To begin with, for our major spend tracking whether demand or supply we rely on marts. Unfortunately, we don’t currently have any mart that provides spend data broken down by objective for either demand or supply.

For supply spend objective-wise distribution, we’re using the {{fleet_campaign_bonus}} explore in Looker. However, this explore is not something we own, and I’m not certain about its validation. That said, it’s currently the only explore available that provides objective-wise spend distribution, and it’s also used in our Supply Cost Breakdown dashboard, so I’ve used the same explore in the new dashboard as well.

Here are some findings using *Paris* as an example:

If you look at the screenshot below, you’ll see that the figure of *€75,754* (actuals) is coming from the {{fleet_campaign_bonus}} view which is exactly what’s used in the Supply Cost Breakdown dashboard.

But when you compare this with the tile titled “[Fleet Campaign Bonus; Breakdown by Spend Objective (Migrated)|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/dashboards/3682?Period+Date=5+week+ago+for+5+week&City+Group+Name=%25Paris%25&Timeframe+Picker=Week&Campaign+Name=&Spend+Objective=&Country+Name=]” in the Supply Cost Breakdown dashboard, the data doesn’t match.

*Why?*
Because in the Supply Cost Breakdown dashboard, we’re applying a filter that includes *only fleet campaigns*.

If you open the [explore|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/explore/rides/fleet_campaign_bonus?qid=NzmV5tSaQ8MTMiY8UGi6gg&toggle=fil,vis] being used in that dashboard and examine the filters, you’ll notice that the {{fleet_campaign}} filter is applied. If you remove that filter, the data will match exactly with the subtotal column for the corresponding week.

!Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 16.39.43.png|width=1385,height=793,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 16.39.43.png"!

!Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 16.19.28.png|width=1422,height=733,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 16.19.28.png"!

*Does the* {{fleet_campaign_bonus}} *Explore work for Tier-3 and metro cities?*

No, currently it does not work correctly for Tier-3 or metro cities. I attempted to adjust the main script to support Tier-3 cities, but unfortunately, it led to double counting issues. One of the challenges is that a single campaign can be used across multiple tests, which complicates attribution?

As a result, for now, only Tier-1 cities are reliably supported in the {{fleet_campaign_bonus}} view.



*Now, moving on to the next point:*

Why is the spend from the mart not matching the spend shown in the {{fleet_campaign_bonus}} Explore?

!Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 16.55.23.png|width=1451,height=789,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 16.55.23.png"!

The main reason for the mismatch is that the supply spend coming from the mart includes all types of spend, such as branding spend and several other categories. You can see this in the mart under the column supply_spend_with_vat_eur, where the full definition covers multiple spend types. In addition to this, the mart also provides separate breakdowns for fleet campaign bonus and branding spend. To understand this better, let’s compare the fleet campaign bonus figures from the [mart|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/explore/curated/metrics_by_region__rides?qid=RP6R9vrJOkWafOAzZ97wJ4&toggle=vis] with the [subtotals in the fleet_campaign_bonus explore|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/explore/rides/fleet_campaign_bonus?qid=ItsPhZVeNFFeRTTUdqLyoH&toggle=fil,vis]: In the mart, we have total supply spend, branding spend, and fleet campaign spend clearly defined. If you compare the fleet campaign spend from the mart with the values in the fleet_campaign_bonus explore, you'll see that the numbers match.

You can also validate this by running the attached script.


{noformat}%sql
SELECT 
  asc2.id,
  asc2.name,
  DATE_TRUNC('week', FROM_UTC_TIMESTAMP(fcb.earned_at, asc2.timezone)) AS earned_at_local,
  --spend_objective,
  SUM(ROUND((fcb.amount / vcer.rate), 4)) AS amount_eur 
FROM ng_public_spark.fleet_campaign_bonus fcb
LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.fleet_campaign_campaign camp ON fcb.campaign_id = camp.id
LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.fleet_driver fd ON fcb.driver_id = fd.id
LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.vw_currency_exchange_rates vcer 
  ON DATE_TRUNC('DAY', vcer.valid_on) = DATE_TRUNC('DAY', fcb.earned_at) AND fcb.currency = vcer.currency
LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.fleet_company fc ON fcb.driver_company_id = fc.id
LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_city asc2 ON fc.city_id = asc2.id
WHERE --fcb.campaign_type = 'fleet_campaign' 
  --AND 
  fcb.sync_state = 'synced' 
  AND asc2.name = 'Paris'
  and (FROM_UTC_TIMESTAMP(fcb.earned_at, asc2.timezone)>=date'2025-06-16' and FROM_UTC_TIMESTAMP(fcb.earned_at, asc2.timezone)<date'2025-07-21')
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3--, 4

{noformat}

!Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 17.17.19.png|width=1458,height=868,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 17.17.19.png"!

!Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 17.07.41.png|width=1667,height=914,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 17.07.41.png"!

So, the key decision we need to make is:

Should we only use the fleet campaign bonus spend (which, in the mart, also includes referral bonuses) — or should we display the full supply spend?

*Do we have referral bonus in spend objective wise distribution?*
Yes, we do have referral bonus appearing in spend objective wise [distribution|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/explore/rides/fleet_campaign_bonus?qid=UuAkPfc6wTJ4NsYBjkFDRj&toggle=fil,vis] as well as we also have referral bonus added in fleet_campaign_bonus_with_vat_eur column coming from mart.

Hi [~accountid:613a01a1e2a0d60069d29ca1] 


The Stanbic Heights lease is +marginally+ more favorable on a few operational points. 

Let me know if you would like a more comprehensive breakdown of what these are. 

Briefly:

* *Reinstatement/Handover* - Stanbic allows landlord to waive reinstatement obligations. OAS gives landlord absolute discretion with no obligation to consider waiver.
* *Relocation/Termination for redevelopment* - Stanbic has a clearer process and explicit continuation of the lease terms in the new space. 
* *Fit-out Process* -  Stanbic offers a more structured and transparent approach to the BO and fit-out handover process compared to the OAS lease, making Stanbic’s terms more balanced and operationally reliable.
* *Use of reasonableness qualifiers on landlord powers* (consent to alterations, use of surety, landlord access to premises, signage approval) - Stanbic includes “reasonableness qualifiers” in these clauses while OAS included no commitment in equivalent clauses. 


Unfortunately both agreements have a similar position on the most pressing issues:

* Liability/indemnity - both are heavily landlord-favorable with no limit/cap
* Termination rights - No early termination right for tenant 
* Early exit - equally rigid 
* Penalities - equal footing

h2. Current Situation

Chatted with *Hannes Mulla* from ProIT. This is the current situation:

* Minimal logging, only what is needed. Additional logging can be enabled when requested and sent where we need.
* Largest part of logging is currently WiFi AP related and already sent to our AWS S3 bucket.
* They are moving from Cisco firewalls to *Fortinet*. Forti sends logs to FortiCloud. Fortinet firewalls are basically router, firewall, DHCP and DNS in one device. There is a firewall in each location, so the number of devices is equal to number of locations, around 30. 
* Physical network ports in our buildings are only connected to the switch for ports where devices that require it are connected (printers, MacMinis, video conferencing devices). Random empty ports provide no connection. If attacker removes an existing device and attaches his device then he would be on a separate VLAN and not able to talk with internal network (TF 5G) where workstations are.
* Hannes could not comment on expected log volume. Depends on what type of logs we want and how detailed, but could go up to a few TB per day. Our current Elastic security cluster storage usage (all time): hot 560 GB, cold 350 GB, frozen 3.63 TB

# *Provide the list of use cases and required log sources to ProIT*. They can figure out how the logs can be forwarded, but we need to provide a destination. Ideally we would send them to S3 bucket. This gives us an option to store more in S3 (cheaper) and apply additional filtering and parsing before logs are forwarded to Elastic.

The user is reporting a double-charge because of incremental authorization.
Incremental authorization in card payments refers to the process of requesting an additional authorization on a customer’s card when the original authorized amount is insufficient to cover the final transaction cost. This typically happens in scenarios where the final amount of the transaction is not known upfront or may change.

I have checked the case and everything looks good on Bolt’s end. The pre-authorization has been released to the customer. 
You can ask the customer to reach out to their bank in order to confirm the authorized funds have been released. Their bank can locate the funds with the authorization date and amount.

CO initial assessment (thought this may change subject to [~accountid:5e2af09cc55f580c9fca70a7]'s response to my follow-up questions above). 

There’s a potential *worker status reclassification risk* if Bolt offers drivers loans to cover the cost of licensing (e.g., £700) and +recovers it through increased commission or other deductions+. The risk turns on whether this scheme, taken with the totality of the driver relationship, *looks more like a dependency or employment-like arrangement*.

Key legal and operational flags from the outset include:

# *Risk of Increased Control or Dependency* 

* *If Bolt advances the money and unilaterally deducts repayment* (e.g., via a higher commission or service fee), it could imply control over the driver’s financial affairs (i.e. worker status).
* *If the scheme is limited to Bolt-platform work*, this may suggest the driver is economically dependent on Bolt, particularly where repayments are structured to require regular platform use.
* If drivers cannot freely choose to *repay early, use third-party funding, or opt out*, HMRC or a tribunal could interpret this as a “benefit” tied to a quasi-employment relationship.

# *Potential financial regulation - CO to check this point with Finance* 

Subject to [~accountid:5e2af09cc55f580c9fca70a7]'s response to my follow-up questions/comments from Finance, if Bolt extends credit and recovers it with interest or charges over time, this may trigger *FCA consumer credit licensing obligations* - unless an exemption applies (e.g., loans interest-free and repayable in ≤12 instalments). We would need to *confirm repayment terms*. 

+Possible Mitigations+ 

Structuring the scheme as an *optional, interest-free advance that is repayable via fixed instalments (not commission rates), without usage or exclusivity conditions* could mitigate reclassification risk. However, if the scheme *limits driver flexibility, links repayment directly to work* (i.e. tying the repayment of the loan to the driver’s activity on the Bolt platform for example by requiring a minimum number of trips per week/month to stay in the scheme), *or alters commission structure,* gives rise to the risk of reclassification.

Hello Team!

I completely understand why this might look like a double charge, but I can assure you that the user was only charged once. This is a common part of how card payments are processed. Here's what happens:

# When the user first makes a payment, the bank temporarily ‘reserves' the funds and this is just the bank setting aside the amount for the transaction. The user’s account balance might show less amount but the payment hasn’t actually been taken out by the bank yet.
# Later, when the payment is fully processed, that reserved amount is now “officially” debited from the user’s account. At that point, some banks send a second notification, which can make it seem like a second charge.


I would advise the user to check their final account balance or statement, where they can confirm that only one payment was actually withdrawn. The earlier “pending” amount will either drop off or convert into the final charge. Also, looking at the Bolt payment descriptor [BOLT.EU/|http://BOLT.EU/x/]X/XXXXXXXXXX, both payments are the same.

Cheers,
Afiba

the necessary data for {{delivery_vertical}} already exists in the fraud system as we are already getting data from provider_trait table. We just need to fetch a new column from it called {{trait_id}}. Once we have the {{trait_id}}we can apply the following SQL to do the proper categorisation:

{code:sql}SELECT
    provider_id,
    CASE WHEN ARRAY_CONTAINS(ARRAY_AGG(trait_id), 42054) AND ARRAY_CONTAINS(ARRAY_AGG(trait_id), 7611) THEN 'market_1p'
    WHEN ARRAY_CONTAINS(ARRAY_AGG(trait_id), 42054) AND ARRAY_CONTAINS(ARRAY_AGG(trait_id), 2441)  THEN 'market_3p_groceries'
    WHEN ARRAY_CONTAINS(ARRAY_AGG(trait_id), 42054) AND ARRAY_CONTAINS(ARRAY_AGG(trait_id), 112481) THEN 'market_3p_retail'
    WHEN ARRAY_CONTAINS(ARRAY_AGG(trait_id), 8224) OR ARRAY_CONTAINS(ARRAY_AGG(trait_id), 8388) THEN 'dine_in'
    ELSE 'food' END AS delivery_vertical
FROM ng_delivery.delivery_provider_provider_trait
GROUP BY 1{code}

To begin with, for our major spend tracking whether demand or supply we rely on marts. Unfortunately, we don’t currently have any mart that provides spend data broken down by objective for either demand or supply.

For supply spend objective-wise distribution, we’re using the {{fleet_campaign_bonus}} explore in Looker. However, this explore is not something we own, and I’m not certain about its validation. That said, it’s currently the only explore available that provides objective-wise spend distribution, and it’s also used in our Supply Cost Breakdown dashboard, so I’ve used the same explore in the new dashboard as well.

Here are some findings using *Paris* as an example:

If you look at the screenshot below, you’ll see that the figure of *€75,754* (actuals) is coming from the {{fleet_campaign_bonus}} view which is exactly what’s used in the Supply Cost Breakdown dashboard.

But when you compare this with the tile titled “[Fleet Campaign Bonus; Breakdown by Spend Objective (Migrated)|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/dashboards/3682?Period+Date=5+week+ago+for+5+week&City+Group+Name=%25Paris%25&Timeframe+Picker=Week&Campaign+Name=&Spend+Objective=&Country+Name=]” in the Supply Cost Breakdown dashboard, the data doesn’t match.

*Why?*
Because in the Supply Cost Breakdown dashboard, we’re applying a filter that includes *only fleet campaigns*.

If you open the [explore|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/explore/rides/fleet_campaign_bonus?qid=NzmV5tSaQ8MTMiY8UGi6gg&toggle=fil,vis] being used in that dashboard and examine the filters, you’ll notice that the {{fleet_campaign}} filter is applied. If you remove that filter, the data will match exactly with the subtotal column for the corresponding week.

!Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 16.39.43.png|width=50%,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 16.39.43.png"!

!Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 16.19.28.png|width=50%,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 16.19.28.png"!

*Does the* {{fleet_campaign_bonus}} *Explore work for Tier-3 and metro cities?*

No, currently it does not work correctly for Tier-3 or metro cities. I attempted to adjust the main script to support Tier-3 cities, but unfortunately, it led to double counting issues. One of the challenges is that a single campaign can be used across multiple tests, which complicates attribution?

As a result, for now, only Tier-1 cities are reliably supported in the {{fleet_campaign_bonus}} view.

 

*Now, moving on to the next point:*

Why is the spend from the mart not matching the spend shown in the {{fleet_campaign_bonus}} Explore?

!Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 16.55.23.png|width=50%,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 16.55.23.png"!

The main reason for the mismatch is that the supply spend coming from the mart includes all types of spend, such as branding spend and several other categories. You can see this in the mart under the column supply_spend_with_vat_eur, where the full definition covers multiple spend types. In addition to this, the mart also provides separate breakdowns for fleet campaign bonus and branding spend. To understand this better, let’s compare the fleet campaign bonus figures from the [mart|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/explore/curated/metrics_by_region__rides?qid=RP6R9vrJOkWafOAzZ97wJ4&toggle=vis] with the [subtotals in the fleet_campaign_bonus explore|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/explore/rides/fleet_campaign_bonus?qid=ItsPhZVeNFFeRTTUdqLyoH&toggle=fil,vis]: In the mart, we have total supply spend, branding spend, and fleet campaign spend clearly defined. If you compare the fleet campaign spend from the mart with the values in the fleet_campaign_bonus explore, you'll see that the numbers match.

You can also validate this by running the attached script.


{noformat}%sql
SELECT 
  asc2.id,
  asc2.name,
  DATE_TRUNC('week', FROM_UTC_TIMESTAMP(fcb.earned_at, asc2.timezone)) AS earned_at_local,
  --spend_objective,
  SUM(ROUND((fcb.amount / vcer.rate), 4)) AS amount_eur 
FROM ng_public_spark.fleet_campaign_bonus fcb
LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.fleet_campaign_campaign camp ON fcb.campaign_id = camp.id
LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.fleet_driver fd ON fcb.driver_id = fd.id
LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.vw_currency_exchange_rates vcer 
  ON DATE_TRUNC('DAY', vcer.valid_on) = DATE_TRUNC('DAY', fcb.earned_at) AND fcb.currency = vcer.currency
LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.fleet_company fc ON fcb.driver_company_id = fc.id
LEFT JOIN ng_public_spark.admin_system_city asc2 ON fc.city_id = asc2.id
WHERE --fcb.campaign_type = 'fleet_campaign' 
  --AND 
  fcb.sync_state = 'synced' 
  AND asc2.name = 'Paris'
  and (FROM_UTC_TIMESTAMP(fcb.earned_at, asc2.timezone)>=date'2025-06-16' and FROM_UTC_TIMESTAMP(fcb.earned_at, asc2.timezone)<date'2025-07-21')
GROUP BY 1, 2, 3--, 4

{noformat}

!Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 17.17.19.png|width=50%,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 17.17.19.png"!

!Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 17.07.41.png|width=50%,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-21 at 17.07.41.png"!

So, the key decision we need to make is:

Should we only use the fleet campaign bonus spend (which, in the mart, also includes referral bonuses) — or should we display the full supply spend?

*Do we have referral bonus in spend objective wise distribution?*
Yes, we do have referral bonus appearing in spend objective wise [distribution|https://bolt.cloud.looker.com/explore/rides/fleet_campaign_bonus?qid=UuAkPfc6wTJ4NsYBjkFDRj&toggle=fil,vis] as well as we also have referral bonus added in fleet_campaign_bonus_with_vat_eur column coming from mart.

Hi [~accountid:5c010fa68ce9b546efc49454] 

I took this ticket over from Natalia. Answering you question:

Renting and using a Bolt scooter (unlocking, riding, returning) is framed as consuming a service through the app in our T&Cs.

The original EU Omnibus Directive is focused primarily on goods, *Poland's implementation includes services also*. The regulation defines services as paid activities, and this includes transportation and rentals.

_“The legislator decided to regulate not only goods, but also services defined in the Law on Price Information.” p. 7 of_ UOKiK Omnibus Explanations.

The *requirement to display the lowest price from the last 30 days* applies *only when* we _inform_ users about a *price reduction* (e.g., in a push or in-app message) - p. 13 _of_ UOKiK Omnibus Explanations.

If the price is simply dynamic and *no reduction is advertised*, the regulation does *not apply*.

“Phrases like ‘promotion’, ‘discount’, ‘cheaper’... mean the trader must show the lowest price from 30 days before the reduction” _p. 15, 39, and 69_ of UOKiK Omnibus Explanations.

|Message|*Allowed*|
|“Unlock a scooter for just 2 PLN”|Only one price is shown. No comparison or discount implied.|
|“Ride anytime, pay per minute”|Describes pricing model, not reduction.|
|“Start your ride from 2.50 PLN”|Neutral phrasing, no suggestion of a price drop.|
|“Dynamic pricing may apply based on demand”|Transparent but not framed as a promotion.|
|“Flat unlock fee applies”|Purely informational.|
|“Enjoy Bolt rides with no surge pricing today”|Describes a feature, not a discount.|

|Message|*Non-Compliant*|
|“Unlock now for only 2 PLN — was 3 PLN!”|Explicit price comparison = price reduction.|
|“-20% off unlock fees today!”|Discount stated = must show previous lowest price.|
|“Cheapest rides of the week!”|Suggests price advantage = must disclose price history.|
|“Reduced unlock fee until Sunday”|"Reduced" triggers legal obligation.|
|“Cheaper unlocks for returning users”|“Cheaper” implies a comparative discount.|
|“Summer discount: unlock at 1.50 PLN”|Must disclose historical lowest price.|

The suggested “_We decreased the price to 0.8PLN/min, unlock price remains the same. Check it out and take a ride with us!” — is not_ compliant with the Polish implementation of the Omnibus Directive unless it is accompanied by the lowest price from the past 30 days for the per-minute fee.

How to make it compliant: “We decreased the price to 0.8 PLN/min (lowest price in last 30 days: 0.9 PLN). Unlock price remains the same. Check it out and take a ride with us!” — This makes the reduction transparent.

“Ride for 0.8 PLN/min. Unlock fee applies.” — This is purely informational, and does not communicate a reduction, so no need to show the lowest 30-day price.



Hope this answers your question!

I would advise to use Annex as a default method in all of the countries (according to ChatGPT and Gemini possible for all of the mentioned countries). Annex shall reference the original contract and confirm that all other terms remain unchanged. From legal side contract is concluded when both parties have signed it so any amendments in the contracts should be made in a way of Annex, not new contract. 

If we see some requests from the local authorities or local legislation to conclude new contract in these cases we can investigate this further for the respective country but Annex approach should be sufficient and best practice for most of the countries (if not all of them) from the list provided.

I would advise to switch from issuing new contract approach to Annex approach ASAP. If we use new contract approach it is absolutely essential that the new contract contains a supersession clause (or "entire agreement clause"). This clause explicitly states that the new agreement replaces and supersedes all prior agreements, whether written or oral, on the subject matter. Without this clause, we risk a situation where a court could find that two contracts are simultaneously valid, leading to significant legal disputes. Issuing a new contract introduces the risk of administrative errors (e.g., old salary data being used, a clause being accidentally omitted).

Excellent point — yes, beyond privacy and data protection, *safety-related robocalls during driving raise broader legal and operational risk considerations*, including *liability, consumer protection, duty of care, and product safety implications*. Here's a full analysis of the *non-privacy legal risks and issues* Bolt should consider before launching such a feature:

----

h2. ⚠️ 1. *Road Safety and Driver Distraction*

h3. a. *Risk of Distracted Driving*

* Robocalls, even safety-related ones, *interrupt the driver’s attention*, which may:
** Increase accident risk (especially at high speeds or in complex traffic situations).
** Conflict with road traffic laws that *prohibit mobile phone use while driving*, unless hands-free.

h3. b. *Legal Consequences*

* *If the call leads to an accident*, the user (or third parties) could claim that:
** Bolt *negligently interfered* with the driver’s ability to operate the vehicle safely.
** The *call was an avoidable distraction*.
* This could create exposure under:
** *Tort law* (negligence claims by injured parties),
** *Product liability law* (arguing that the Drive service was defectively designed),
** *Contractual claims* (if the user suffers loss and argues the robocall was unreasonably intrusive).

h3. c. *Recommended Safeguards*

* Ensure the call is *hands-free compatible* and ideally designed to *connect to the car’s infotainment system*.
* Keep messages *extremely short and pre-recorded*, with no user input required.
* *Avoid two-way interactions* (no IVR prompts like "press 1 to acknowledge").
* Consider *delaying or suppressing the robocall* in high-risk contexts (e.g. extreme speed, sharp turns, city congestion).

----

h2. 📵 2. *Conflict With Local Traffic Laws*

h3. a. *Phone Use While Driving Laws*

* Many countries prohibit the use of *mobile devices while driving*, even hands-free in some cases.
** *Germany*, *France*, *Spain*, and others impose fines or liability on distracted driving.
* Bolt triggering a call — even for a good reason — could be seen as encouraging or facilitating prohibited conduct.

h3. b. *Possible Mitigating Measures*

* Include *language in the message* advising drivers not to take the call if it’s unsafe.
* Add in-app *advance notice* that robocalls may occur, and users must obey road rules (e.g. stop before listening).

----

h2. 📄 3. *Duty of Care and Negligence Risk*

h3. a. *Duty of Care Towards Users*

* As a mobility platform, Bolt owes a *duty of care* to users of its services.
* Interventions like robocalls change the risk landscape — Bolt may be held to a *higher standard of care* if it:
** Initiates interventions during dangerous situations,
** Fails to foresee that the intervention may *cause more harm than it prevents*.

h3. b. *Foreseeability and Proximate Cause*

* If an incident occurs immediately after or during a robocall, plaintiffs may argue:
** It was *foreseeable* that a call would distract the driver.
** The call was a *proximate cause* of the incident.

h3. c. *Mitigation Strategies*

* Include *clear disclaimers* (in T&Cs and voice message) that driver remains responsible for safe driving.
* Consider *indemnification clauses* in rental T&Cs to reduce exposure (though enforceability varies).
* Carefully *log robocall timing and trigger conditions*, in case of future legal scrutiny.

----

h2. 📢 4. *Consumer Protection and Fairness*

* Automated interventions can be challenged under *unfair commercial practices law* if:
** They are *disproportionately intrusive*,
** Users are *not clearly informed*,
** Or they affect the *quality or safety of the service*.

Especially in B2C contexts, the *balance of rights and obligations* must be transparent.

----

h2. 🧠 5. *Psychological and UX Impact*

While not strictly legal, poor execution can create *user backlash* or reputational damage:

* Robocalls may come across as *patronising*, *annoying*, or even *stress-inducing* while driving.
* Frequent alerts may erode trust and lead to *abandonment of the service* or *bad publicity*.
* If users feel monitored or penalised without consent, *regulatory complaints* may follow — even outside of strict legal violations.

----

h2. 🔧 6. Product Design Risk (Safety vs. Enforcement)

* A robocall may be perceived as a *quasi-enforcement action* — i.e. not just a reminder, but a warning.
* This introduces questions of:
** *What happens after the call?*
** Is Bolt logging the incident for future action (e.g. banning, penalties)?
** How does this affect *user appeal rights*, *dispute resolution*, or *complaint procedures*?

Poor process design may be challenged under *fairness principles* in consumer and contract law.

----

h2. ✅ Risk Mitigation Summary

||Risk Category||Recommended Controls||
|*Driver Distraction*|Ensure hands-free, very short calls; avoid complex IVR; allow opt-out where possible.|
|*Traffic Law Conflicts*|Warn users to only take calls when safe; geofence jurisdictions with high legal risk.|
|*Negligence/Liability*|Include disclaimers in T&Cs; monitor call timing; log interventions for audit.|
|*Consumer Protection*|Make purpose, frequency, and process very clear; offer reasonable user control.|
|*UX/Reputational Risk*|Pilot test in low-risk markets; collect user feedback; iterate on tone and frequency.|

----

h2. Conclusion

While the *intent is safety*, Bolt must be careful not to *inadvertently increase legal exposure* by intervening at the wrong time, in the wrong way. Robocalls are highly regulated, and their real-time nature adds *behavioural, legal, and operational complexity*.









Thank you – that clarification is very helpful. Given that the *robocalls are safety alerts*, aimed at *prompting real-time behavioural correction* (e.g. asking drivers to stop speeding), the legal framing becomes more defensible — but still subject to scrutiny under *GDPR* and *ePrivacy* rules. Below is a revised legal analysis focused on *compliance, risk mitigation, and stakeholder readiness*.

----

h2. ⚖️ 1. Legal Qualification of the Robocall

Although the *purpose is safety*, which can support a *legitimate interest* argument, the *medium used* (automated calling) still triggers regulatory scrutiny under national ePrivacy laws. Importantly:

* *Robocalls without human intervention* are treated as *electronic communications*, regulated separately from the GDPR.
* In most EU Member States, even non-marketing robocalls *require prior consent* due to their intrusiveness — *regardless of purpose*.

Thus, while the _content_ is safety-oriented, the _channel_ (automated voice call) remains legally sensitive.

----

h2. 📜 2. Legal Bases for Data Processing

h3. a. *Primary Basis: Legitimate Interests (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR)*

* Processing driver data (speed, phone number) is likely *necessary for the purpose of ensuring safety* and preventing accidents.
* Your *interest in promoting safe driving* and *preventing harm* can outweigh the limited intrusion _if proper safeguards are in place_.

📝 You must conduct and document a *Legitimate Interests Assessment (LIA)*, covering:

* Purpose necessity (why this alert method?),
* Minimal intrusiveness (e.g. short message, non-repetitive),
* Balance of interests (user rights vs. Bolt’s duty of care).

h3. b. *Alternative: Contractual Necessity (Art. 6(1)(b))*

* Possible if users explicitly accept real-time safety contact as part of the rental agreement.
* But this basis is narrow — it must be _strictly necessary_ to deliver the service.

----

h2. 📞 3. ePrivacy Compliance – Robocalls

Even if the purpose is safety:

* *Germany, France, Italy, Austria, Spain, etc.*: Robocalls still require *explicit prior consent* under national laws implementing the *ePrivacy Directive*.
* *Some Nordic or Baltic countries* may allow *legitimate interest for non-marketing robocalls*, but the trend is conservative.

✅ *Best practice*:

* *Request opt-in during onboarding* for safety-related calls (robocalls, not just push notifications).
* Or, implement the system in *phased roll-out*, with *geo-fencing* where consent is not required.

----

h2. 🔍 4. Transparency, Notices & User Control

Regardless of legal basis, Bolt must *clearly inform users*:

* That driving behaviour (e.g. speeding) is monitored.
* That safety-related automated calls may be triggered in response.
* Why the measure is in place (prevent harm, ensure compliance).
* That calls are *not marketing*.
* How to *opt out* (if allowed under legal basis).

*Update the following:*

* Bolt Drive Privacy Policy
* Rental Terms
* In-app notices
* Consent flows (if needed)

----

h2. ⚙️ 5. Technical & Organisational Safeguards

If using a *third-party calling solution*:

* Sign a *DPA* (Art. 28 GDPR).
* Ensure *data minimisation*: Only pass the required fields (e.g. phone number + limited driving trigger).
* No retention of robocall content unless legally necessary.
* Calls should be *short*, *non-repetitive*, and *clearly safety-related*.

----

h2. 📍 6. Country-by-Country Practical Risk Notes

||Country||Consent Required for Robocalls?||Notes||
|*Germany*|Yes|Very strict; clear opt-in needed, even for safety|
|*France*|Yes|Consent required for automated voice; SMS alternative might be easier|
|*Estonia*|Possibly No|Easier for service messages; confirm with local DPO|
|*Italy*|Yes|Robocalls only allowed with consent|
|*Spain*|Yes|Conservative interpretation; safer with opt-in|
|*Finland*|Maybe not|Non-marketing may be allowed under legitimate interest|
|*Poland*|Yes|Consent-based; enforced by telecom regulator|
|*Sweden*|Possibly No|Subject to data protection balancing test|

----

h2. 📌 7. DPIA Consideration

This use case likely requires a *Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA)* under Article 35 GDPR, due to:

* *Systematic monitoring of driver behaviour*,
* *Automated decision triggers* (robocall based on a rule),
* *Potential impact on users’ rights*.

Structure your DPIA to show:

* Safety benefit,
* Risk mitigation (non-invasive design, opt-out, consent if needed),
* Technical controls (logging, access restriction, deletion policies).

----

h2. ✅ Key Recommendations Summary

||Topic||Recommendation||
|*GDPR Basis*|Use *legitimate interest*, with LIA and strong justification.|
|*ePrivacy Compliance*|Implement *consent* for robocalls where legally required.|
|*User Notice*|Update all user-facing materials; be transparent and proactive.|
|*DPIA*|Complete a DPIA with DPO oversight.|
|*Consent Design*|Build consent flows into Bolt Drive onboarding; explain purpose clearly.|
|*Rollout Strategy*|Consider *geo-targeted pilot* in permissive jurisdictions.|
|*Fallback Channel*|Consider less intrusive alternatives (e.g. *push or SMS*) where robocalls are too risky.|

Hi [~accountid:712020:b9ff5ee8-46de-4250-9860-5a4361d842fa] 

That’s a good point from the customers point of view. 

There are multiple teams involved. 
The way this works is that a customer makes an order request. Booking is created by the ride hailing vertical. 
The Ride Hailing team is requesting the Customer payments team to create a payment through API. The Fraud team assigns a pre-authorization amount. 

When the payment gets cancelled then Bolt immediately releases the pre-authorization. In Most EU countries the pre-authorization is released to the customer within minutes. In some countries it can take up to 30 days. 

Please also keep in mind that the pre-authorization is not a charge as the funds never leave the customers account. It’s a reservation. 

You can provide the customer the acquirer references to locate and confirm the authorized funds have been released.

This can happen when a user purchases a pass and places a rental order within a very short timespan (less than one minute). The scooter pass payment takes some time to settle, and if it hasn’t settled yet, the user’s Bolt balance becomes negative.

As a result, the user is prompted to pay off their negative balance during the rental order, which leads to a double charge. Once the pass payment settles, the funds are returned to the user's Bolt balance.

We fixed 98% of these cases back in May, but it looks like this user is still affected.

1. We are not collecting this data as part of application. By “before the employment” I mean after the applicant has accepted the offer and we collect the information we need for the employment. Our team currently doesn’t have a process to delete these records once an employee has been onboarded. This is the input I have from the local People Partner:
Under the *Polish Labour Code (Kodeks pracy)*, and the *Regulation of the Minister of Family, Labour and Social Policy of December 10, 2018*, employers are entitled to collect specific documents *only at designated stages of the employment process*.
According to § 3 of the Regulation:

* *Copies of diplomas, certificates, etc.* should be collected *only once the candidate has been selected and offered a role*, i.e., *at the hiring stage*, if necessary to confirm qualifications.

*For Hired Employees – Part of Personnel Files*
If diplomas, certificates, or other documents were collected *after the candidate was hired* and used to *confirm qualifications*, then:

* They must be stored in *Section B of the personnel file*, as specified in the regulation:

*§ 3(2)(2)(a) of the Regulation of December 10, 2018*
 “Section B of the personnel file includes documents relating to the establishment of the employment relationship, including documents confirming professional qualifications.”

* These documents are subject to the general employee file retention period:

*Article 94⁵ § 2 of the Polish Labour Code*
 “Employee documentation must be stored for 10 years from the end of employment (for contracts signed after January 1, 2019).”



# In the Polish context, the medical documents in question refer to referrals to occupational health examinations (_skierowania na badania lekarskie_), and occupational health certificates (_orzeczenia lekarskie_) confirming whether the employee is fit to work on a given position.
These documents are required under the *Polish Labour Code* and *occupational health regulations*. Employers are obligated to:
## *Refer employees to medical checks* (pre-employment, periodic, and return-to-work after medical leave),
## *Obtain a formal certificate* from an occupational physician confirming if the employee is fit or unfit to perform duties at a specific role and exposure level (e.g., computer work, night shifts, hazardous conditions).


Occupational medical certificates must be kept, as it confirms if the employee is medically fit for their job. It contains no sensitive diagnosis, only a decision: _fit / unfit to work_, it is a mandatory part of personnel documentation and it must be retained for the duration of employment + 10 years.

Medical referral – No legal obligation to keep permanently. So if needed, we can proceed with not storing these.

*Update: DPA Review with WorldPay*

We had multiple discussions with WorldPay on the DPA and we are finally close to an agreement, but a few things are still being discussed.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
Below is a summary of the key outstanding issues and associated risks:

* *Notification of New Sub-Processors*
WorldPay intends to notify Bolt via its internal portal instead of by email. This may be considered unlawful under GDPR due to lack of active notice and insufficient visibility.
*Risk*: Bolt may lose effective control over WorldPay’s outsourcing decisions.
* *Bolt Infosec Code of Practice*
Bolt does not require full adherence but expects a commitment to “similar protection” per its standard DPA wording. WorldPay refused and wants to rely solely on its own policies, with no reference to Bolt’s Infosec Code.
*Risk*: Security standards may not be fully aligned with Bolt’s without Bolt’s infosec confirmation of custom measures, though overall risk is low given WorldPay’s regulated status.
* *Liability for Sub-Processor Objections*
Bolt’s position is that if it objects to a new sub-processor, it should be able to terminate affected services without liability and receive a refund of prepaid fees (if applicable). WorldPay rejected this entirely.
*Risk*: In case of disagreement, Bolt is only protected under general contract terms with a liability cap and no refund.
* *Separate Liability for Data Protection Matters*

Yes, we can remove Bolt Boost payments from Ltd company fleets. I’m currently updating the UK Principal Service Provider Terms and could build this in the current draft. 

In the context of Odysse, we should probably have a conversation with them first just to avoid any friction from going straight from paying to not paying Bolt Boost. 

*Why this helps legally -* not paying Bolt Boost to fleet drivers reinforces the position that Bolt is contracting with a business (the fleet), not with the individual drivers. That separation helps reduce worker reclassification risk by distancing Bolt from any perceived control over driver pay.

*What to keep in mind -* the commercial downside is that this could potentially increase our financial exposure in the event the fleet drivers successfully bring a work status claim against us. However, if the fleet properly employs its drivers, and we don’t take direct enforcement action against individuals, the risk of reclassification is low.

Hello,

The deposit is technically considered as a preauthorisation amount which is later returned to the user few days after the order completion. In this case, the payment was reverse on July 8 and should reflect back in the user’s payment method after 14 days (maximum 30 days) according to the user’s bank internal processes. The user can check the transaction state with their bank by providing them with the date and the amount of the charge.



Banks work differently and while some might release the preauthorisation immediately after the order completion, some might process the preauthorisation as an actual charge and then refund it later to the customers, which can take a longer processing time. 

Unfortunately, we do not have full visibility on all the parties included in the payment processing. We can only confirm with our payment partner that they sent out the preauthorisation amount, but taking into account the acquirers and other payments services/network involved in the process, we can’t check where the preauthorisation release state is currently at.
We are sorry for the inconvenience caused to the customers but most of the time the reversal is completed after 30 days as pending payments on banks' end automatically expire after that time.

Hello,

Banks work differently and while some might release the preauthorisation immediately after the order completion, some might process the preauthorisation as an actual charge and then refund it later to the customers, which can take a longer processing time. 

Unfortunately, we do not have full visibility on all the parties included in the payment processing. We can only confirm with our payment partner that they sent out the preauthorisation amount, but taking into account the acquirers and other payments services/network involved in the process, we can’t check where the preauthorisation release state is currently at.
We are sorry for the inconvenience caused to the customers but most of the time the reversal is completed after 30 days as pending payments on banks' end automatically expire after that time.

As a first step, I’ve pulled all the orders from the driver to determine which strategies were responsible for affecting his NLW top-up. 

For this driver, only one rule was triggering: [LOW_ORDER_FINISHED_RATIO|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/fraud/rules/edit/rides_driver_payout_benefits_abuse/LOW_ORDER_FINISHED_RATIO?configTab=config_view&tab=basic]

Driver’s weekly stats:

!Screenshot 2025-07-23 at 10.00.16.png|width=390,height=157,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-23 at 10.00.16.png"!

Manually checked some examples to validate if it was visible that the driver was accepting trips with no intent of actually doing them. Noticed multiple cases where the rider’s ETA was pretty large and the order would end up being cancelled rather quickly, which made me wonder if the driver was legit and not at fault for these cancellations. To be clear, the reason I considered the driver to be legitimate was that he had a fairly decent volume of finished rides as well, and some of them were concluded despite the high ETA. 

Some high ETA cancellation examples:
[https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/581318696/25|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/581318696/25?orderTryId=1300600961]
[https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/580287526/25|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/580287526/25?orderTryId=1291957707]
[https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/580855526/25|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/580855526/25?orderTryId=1296704669]

Finished orders with high ETA:
[https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/578463320/25|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/578463320/25]
[https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/578536757/25|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/578536757/25]
[https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/580944049/25|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/580944049/25?orderTryId=1297516463]

As a next step, decide to check July’s aggregated data for the driver. 

!Screenshot 2025-07-23 at 10.19.57.png|width=50%,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-23 at 10.19.57.png"!

92% of his cancellations have an ETA higher than 10 minutes. Hundreds of them. 

!Screenshot 2025-07-23 at 10.21.08.png|width=1069,height=105,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-23 at 10.21.08.png"!

If you look at his finished orders, only 8.5% of the finished orders had an ETA higher than 10 minutes. That doesn’t necessarily tell us much, as it makes sense that longer ETA rides end up being more cancelled than finished. But what we can see here is that the higher ETA rides have a higher avg GMV as well, which is also logical, most drivers should be trying to make a profit on our platform, and to compensate for longer pickups, you need expensive rides. What we can also observe is that in the whole month of July, the driver never finished an order with an ETA higher than 20 minutes; he had over 500 cancellations of them.   

The profitability angle can also be observed for all drivers in GB:

!Screenshot 2025-07-23 at 10.25.35.png|width=1068,height=144,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-23 at 10.25.35.png"!

The higher the ETA, the higher the avg GMV per ride is. Only 0.04% of rides were ever finished with an ETA higher than 30 minutes and with an avg GMV of £74 per trip. 

Looking further at our driver, we see that he accepted multiple rides with an ETA higher than 40 minutes with a very marginal price, which is a clear sign that he didn’t intend to do these trips. He only accepts them because he’s aware that they’ll be cancelled and he’ll get paid by Bolt through the NLW benefit without having to move after accepting these rides. Here are some examples:
[https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/579081617/25|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/579081617/25]
[https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/579042802/25|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/579042802/25]
[https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/579051465/25|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/ride-hailing-order/orders/order/579051465/25]

Finally, we can also see that the driver’s acceptance rate dropped significantly after we launched the NLW benefits, which corroborates that he’s only accepting these trips because we’re paying him. 

!Screenshot 2025-07-23 at 14.44.07.png|width=958,height=726,alt="Screenshot 2025-07-23 at 14.44.07.png"!

The conclusion is that the driver is accepting trips with no intent of doing them, and therefore, our action was justified. We won’t adjust his top-up compensation further.

Law no. 363/2007 on combating unfair commercial practices (transposing EU Directive 2005/29/EC) and Law no. 158/2008 on misleading and comparative advertising (transposing EU Directive 2006/114/EC) prohibit misleading advertising, whether through actions or omissions, especially those that:

* Distort the economic behavior of the _average consumer_; or
* Lead the _average consumer_ to believe they are receiving a financial benefit that is not real or substantiated.

Accordingly, to ensure compliance with the above legal provisions, it is advisable that:

* The annual price reflects *all costs* that must be borne by the consumer in connection with the service (including any applicable taxes, fees, or administrative charges);
* Advertisements are *clearly and prominently identified as such*, (e.g., by labeling them as “Ad” or “Advertisement”);
* Phrases such as “Members usually save X RON” or “Save up to X RON” are used only when based on *accurate, average, or representative data that can be objectively verified*;

Failure to comply with these requirements may expose Bolt to sanctions for misleading advertising, ranging from RON 10,000 to RON 100,000, applied by ANPC.

In addition to the above requirements regarding advertising, consumers must be provided with a clear and timely opportunity to opt out before any automatic subscription renewal (consider informing users in advance when a subscription is set to renew).

This failure is caused by exchange rate not in {{vw_currency_exchange_rates}} table when the LTV pipeline runs. There could be two ways to address this issue:

# we could use the currency rate from the day before computed_on date.
# according to this [thread|https://taxify.slack.com/archives/C036MJC2YG1/p1753269183011149?thread_ts=1753268025.501249&cid=C036MJC2YG1], the currency_rates are updated every ~3.5 hours, we could delay our current pipeline by a few hours.

I personally prefer the first way, as it’s less error prone. The downside is it may lead to small deviations.

With regards to why after relaunching the job on airflow, model training still fails with the same error. It’s because whenever query step is executed, it appends the output to S3 (line 276 and 288 in this [file|https://github.com/bolteu/data-science/blob/master/sagemaker-jenkins/rider-ltv-predictor-v1/src/steps/query/query.py]). In this way, the corrupted data was never removed or overwritten. A simple fix is to change the value of mode parameter from ‘append' to 'overwrite’.

This data [here|https://eu-central-1.console.aws.amazon.com/s3/buckets/taxify-datascience-sagemaker?region=eu-central-1&bucketType=general&prefix=mlpipelines/rider-ltv-predictor-v1/2025-06-16+02%3A00%3A00%2B00%3A00/query/output/computed_on%3D2025-06-23/query_name%3Dtrain_flv/&showversions=false] is an example how data is appended but not overwritten. (multiple dates in last_modified column corresponds multiple pipeline relaunches on airflow)

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt is entering into a partnership with MOL in the context of Bolt Rewards.
** Apparently it is very unlikely that the contractual provisions will change. Hence red-flag review.
* [Partnership Agreement|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TcFVuTxUExph0E7tHpCI9b9SpRUN5VXe/edit]:
** Between Polish Bolt entity and Polish MOL entity.
** Sets out principal terms of participation in the Bolt loyalty program. MOL will be providing services to Bolt drivers (i.e., discounts on fuel and car services), which will be offered to drivers via the Bolt platform.
*** Bolt is effectively providing ‘visibility services’ here - presenting MOL services to Bolt drivers on the platform. Explicitly framed in terms of marketing (“_The Partner acknowledges that the BOLT App or BOLT Platform is considered a marketing channel used to inform Drivers about the services or benefits and discounts related to such goods and/or services provided by the Partner_”).
** Only mentions the following data processing
*** Clause 5:
**** Bolt can use metrics and data relating to Bolt Rewards Program to improve them and make case studies.
**** Bolt can provide MOL with aggregated data relating to Bolt Rewards Program.
*** Clause 11:
**** Parties are independent data controllers.
**** If Parties decide to share driver data, they will enter into a DSA.
** MOL indemnifies Bolt for any breach of laws (pretty broad).
* Apparently there are two points highlighted in red that need review - I cannot see these.

+*THOUGHTS*+

* No immediate concerns with the PA terms from a privacy POV, but I have no visibility on what data is being shared here. If driver personal data is being shared, the agreement explicitly requires a DSA.
* Also unclear how this will be marketed to drivers. If direct marketing is involved, I should include the usual advice (e.g., [+LSS-52286+|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-52286]).

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** Has the red highlight been removed?
** What data is being shared here, in what direction, and for what purpose?
** If data is being shared, presumably it is just between these entities and not with any third parties?
** Presumably a DSA has not already been entered with this party?
** How will this be marketed to the drivers?
* If driver data is being shared in a non-aggregated form, we need a DSA.
* If direct marketing applies here, then usual advice applies.

** Where we are using *targeted* means (e.g., emails, push notifications, in-app comms) to encourage Bolt drivers to use MOL’s services, we should only do so for users that have *consented* to receiving comms about third-party products and services.
*** Where we are promoting MOL’s services to Bolt drivers via *untargeted* means (e.g., banners and webpages, not at specific users / user categories), we *do not* need to obtain user consent.
** In the comms, we should always provide drivers with the option to *unsubscribe* from them. We are likely doing this already, but just flagging for completness.

Hello [~accountid:5b7bea09d08e47445d6fd01e]!

The TVDE Driver certificate is issued by the IMT, according to article 10.º, n.º 2, d) of TVDE Law.

I see all three certificates attached have different registry numbers, therefore, either 2 of them are fake or all 3 are fake.

Manufacturing a fake document, falsifying a existing document or altering any of the elements that constitute such documents, presenting or possessing such documents by any means, are all conducts that can be considered a crime of counterfeiting or forgery of documents, as per article 256.º of the Portuguese Penal Code.

This crime is regarded as a public crime, which means that Bolt can, on its own, present a criminal complaint to the Public Prosecutor against the person who presented these 3 documents, so that an investigation is conducted to assess the veracity of the documents and determine responsibility for the crime.

In this regard, it should also be pointed out that, as per article 14.º of TVDE Law, Bolt has a duty to ensure compliance of all the requirements regarding drivers, blocking them when they are in breach (which I know we are already doing in these cases).

However, considering that the documents are issued by the IMT, its ultimately this entity that can absolutely confirm wether or not it has issued such documents and if they are forged or counterfeit.

Therefore, despite Bolt’s possibility to move forward with criminal complaint, I would recommend that we first seek counsel with the IMT on how they wish to approach this issue, considering they may prefer to be the ones to present the claim, with Bolt’s assistance.
