There are two ways we can use the Mapbox SDK to highlight a building:

# Using {{setFilter}} like in [this|https://docs.mapbox.com/mapbox-gl-js/example/using-box-queryrenderedfeatures/] example. We would have to have two separate building layers: a _default_ layer, and a _selected_ layer. The _default_ layer would be active all the time and have the standard styling. The _selected_ layer would have a different styling and we would always apply a filter such that only the target building(s) would be visible.
# Using {{setFeatureState}} like in [this|https://docs.mapbox.com/mapbox-gl-js/example/hover-styles/] example. Here we would have to define a "selected" state for the building layer. When required, we would simply set the "selected" state to true for the target building.

The second option seems the more elegant solution, since we don't have to define and maintain two separate layers in Mapbox Studio.

Unfortunately, neither of these options is supported by the rn-mapbox [package|https://github.com/rnmapbox/maps]. Support for the {{setFeatureState}} function is added in [this|https://github.com/rnmapbox/maps/pull/3741] PR, but it hasn't been reviewed since January.

However, it looks like we might have a more straight-forward way of implementing this.

Since the building entrance detection model is trained on OSM footprints, we can modify it to return, alongside the prediction, the {{way}} id of the building (this would be required for the SDK option anyway). We can also have it return, at least in the prototype phase, the list of points (encoded in a certain way - perhaps in the Google polyline format) that make up the building footprint.
As a side note - we can use the model for merchants as well.

We can then serve the list of points to the Courier app, which will simply paint the polygon on the map. Since, in general, the source for Mapbox footprints is also OSM, the overlay should look good.

*Limitations*:

* the model only has predictions for 75%-ish of the cases. Out of those, we will not be able to use the {{UNBOUND_DELIVERY_SPOT}} prediction types, since they are... not bound to a building
* the model only works for {{way}}s , not {{relations}}. We can consider including {{relation}}s as well to increase the model coverage
* for the prototype we should only enable the feature in a few cities, since memory consumption might increase too much from the extra data

*Steps post-prototyping:*


Instead of keeping the polyline in the model, we can keep only the way/relation id and leverage the {{map-elements}} service to get the footprint.
However, currently {{map-elements}} does not import buildings, so we'll have to update the importing step to also include them. This should be fairly easy to achieve though.

Another idea is to export everything (entrances and building footprints) into a custom data-layer, built specifically for our use case.

To increase our coverage beyond the 75% (i.e. not to depend solely on the entrance model), a more complex solution is required: some sort of smart-reverse-geocoding, where we search for buildings within a radius of the delivery location and try to match based on multiple things (e.g. address, address notes etc.). This is highly speculative and likely not worth implementing.

Caveats

* Watch out for nodes that represent entrances like in here [https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/26884804.|https://www.openstreetmap.org/way/26884804.] They should not be encoded into the polyline.

Hi [~accountid:712020:459f4dab-1b84-4b5a-8aec-5b1cfceef16b] this feature has been reviewed by the Product Legal team and myself. Please find below our assessment:

The feature introduces a new ride category for drivers without changing our contracts or how we pay them. Since drivers are auto-enrolled (but can opt out) and we’re clearly communicating the feature, the legal risk is manageable.

*Key Points:*

* *Driver Contracts:*
No need to change our current Terms & Conditions. Everything can be handled in-app.
* *Transparency for Riders and Drivers:*
We need to clearly explain how this category works — especially how rides are ranked, priced, and how drivers can opt out. This keeps us compliant with platform rules.
* *No Risk of Employment Reclassification:*
Because we’re not changing how we manage or control drivers, this feature doesn’t increase the risk of drivers being seen as employees.
* *Fleet Drivers:*
Fleet Owners must also receive the same emails as their drivers — this keeps us consistent with what we’ve agreed with them.
* *Price Bidding:*
Please make sure that we are not planning to test the feature where riders and drivers can “bid” for rides — that would conflict with the logic of the priority model.
* *Rider Comms – Be Careful with Wording:*
Don’t call this a “booking fee” or suggest riders are paying to jump the queue. That kind of language could be misleading.

* *Contractual Parties:* The vehicle leasing contract is between Bolt Services DE GmbH and Volkswagen Leasing GmbH, while Jacobs Automobile acts only as an intermediary and not as a contractual party, which supports the option that a change of the executing dealership is possible if Volkswagen Leasing agrees.
* *Change of Dealership:* While we have to accept delivery at the agreed handover point (§ I.7.1 Rahmenvertrag, which could be interpreted as Jacobs Dealership), I currently see no clause prohibiting Volkswagen Leasing GmbH from changing the sourcing dealership before issuing the Bereitstellungsanzeige. * *Process:* We do not unilaterally have the power to direct such a change, only Volkswagen Leasing, as the purchaser and owner, could potentially  internally reallocate the dealership, unless Jacobs is contractually guaranteed the execution by Volkswagen Leasing.
* *Conclusion:* Legally, rerouting the dealership before handover could be viable and does not trigger the 15% non-acceptance penalty, as long as we do not reject delivery, the lease terms remain unchanged, and Volkswagen Leasing  agrees to this particular change.

* On July 14, a Bolt employee fell victim to a phishing attack (by clicking a link in an email). The employee then mistakenly approved an OKTA MFA request, which enabled the attackers to log into the employee's Greenhouse Account.
* This access to Greenhouse was used to send job ads to over 100,000 e-mail addresses, including phishing links that were designed to steal Google account credentials.
* From InfoSec's investigation, the recipient list was uploaded by the attacker and not taken from Bolt's systems.
* InfoSec is working with Greenhouse to ensure better technical measures for alerts for unusual activity on the account, including anomalous volumes of emails sent.
* Privacy and InfoSec will be working with Recruitment to audit Greenhouse 'roles and permissions' to prevent similar future incidents.
* Privacy reported the incident to the Estonian Data Protection Inspectorate (AKI) on 24.07 and are working on Data Breach Notifications to the affected recipients with the LCM Team.

The logic is as follows:

* In reality – we get some result, which is ({{delta_from_curve}} + noise). We also get credible/ confidence intervals, which show where the actual original_delta should be (given by noise, which is estimated during the experiment)
* Here, we do the inverse: we know the {{delta_from_curve}}. We add some noise based on the credible/confidence intervals. By the end of the day, the model receives estimate in the form of {{delta_from_curve}} +noise (with credible intervals necessarily encapsulate the actual effect)
* One only allowance that we are making here is that we are measuring sigmas using percentage (and not in absolutes)
** If we did it in real life, percentage would depend on whether delta>{{delta_from_curve}} or delta<{{delta_from_curve}} (because with percentage we are taking a very lower/higher base)
** But this should not impact our measurements drastically (sigma-s are still somewhat directional)
** Reminder: percentage is necessary, because the model checks different kinds of vmax, big and small. Our experiments could be showing low vmax (and therefore lower sigmas), but it would be unfair to pick those sigmas for very high vmax-s.

One more question:

* should when assigning the “noise“, should we do it with Uniform or Normal distribution
** Normal seems to be more aligned with Meta and Quasi-experiments (where we have Bayesian estimates) – this would make our results more optimistic, divergences would not be as small.
** Uniform is more about frequentist approach (Google CLS). Going for Uniform approach everywhere would also make the studies more conservative.

h2. Important

After testing the calculator flow on a *one-week long Global AA time-slice test*, the volume of enrollments was too big so that after 2 hours of working, the cluster was dying because of executor dying and deleting stage artifacts so that the spark job could never recover. After changing the cluster to non-photon, with bigger executors (64 GB memory), the cluster was dying after 10 hours of processing because of lack of local disk space to store the shuffling artifacts. Of course, the biggest problem here is the query complexity—the joins in particular.

Thus, if we need to compute such a big artifact, we need to *batch process the AA test with up to 25 cities per run spread equally*. This will allow us to get one partial artifact in *2-3 hours* (depending if CUPED is enabled or not).

Given that we have 25 cities per batch, we will need 20-30 job runs, which is *40-90 hours* of computing for a single global artifact.

I continued testing on the C2 frames by finding where is the interference was. 

!image-20250724-133916.png|width=1043,height=1391,alt="image-20250724-133916.png"!

_Almost brand new C2 frame. Battery does not go further down without big force applied to it_ ⬆️

!image-20250724-135627.png|width=1043,height=1391,alt="image-20250724-135627.png"!

_Another C2. Same as above_ ⬆️  

Before testing anything else, I took a C2 battery and put it into the same scooters. There were no issues, C2 battery worked perfectly.

At first I removed the battery lock to make testing faster and also make sure the lock does not cause any sticking. As removing the lock did not change anything, I continued to find the interference by using spray paint to cover the battery tower on the inside and then run the battery in and out of the tower a couple of times to see where the paint wears off.

This way I could identify that the interference is *only on the guide ribs of the battery*. On all frames I tested, the phenomena was exactly the same. There was no contact with the tower at any other location. 

To verify my theory, I took a narrow belt sander and polished down the side ribs. It took quite a while to get a good result, but it was very clear that the more I sanded, the smaller the resistance got. I repeated the painting step a few times during the sanding process to see how much more I need to sand.

!image-20250724-135811.png|width=1437,height=755,alt="image-20250724-135811.png"!



*After polishing down both side ribs, the problem disappeared and and battery went in super smoothly.* 

*I repeated the test on another frame and result was exactly the same.* (/) 

On the third frame I did not sand anything, but instead I used tire installation grease on the sides of the battery and that also solved the issue. Battery went in smoothly and was able to be removed without excess force. It was still interfering, but moved without major effort. Unfortunately that does not seem a viable option for real operations, as the grease will start collecting dust very soon and also the greased batteries will be very messy. But maybe it can be used as a workaround to unstick batteries that are already stuck by dripping spray grease into the tower. *I asked local team to test this next time they encounter the problem.* 

I also tested 4 brand new out of the box C2 frames. 2 frames were completely problem free, one was very slightly sticking in the bottom and the last one got stuck in the bottom of the tower, right where the welds on the outer surface of the battery tower are. Not as bad as the samples local team had selected, but still stuck. Check video.

!PXL_20250723_142615123.mp4|width=1080,height=1920,alt="PXL_20250723_142615123.mp4"!

!image-20250724-140529.png|width=670,height=683,alt="image-20250724-140529.png"!

Next up I compared the C3 housing to the C2 housing to find out why the C3 gets stuck. 

I managed to measure that the whole battery is 0.5~0.7mm wider, which also pushes the bottoms of the guide ribs out and makes them stick in frames where towers are slightly narrower, either due to welding or extrusion tolerances. (x) 



After testing the things above, local team brought out a C3 battery that had been very heavily used (it used to be a test battery for the mechanics, averaging 30-40 in-out cycles daily. I tried it in the third C2 I had not modified and it went in and came out without big effort. It was still sticking, but could be pulled out by hand.

I also measured that test battery and found that

# the side guides are deeper due to wear. It is hard to measure precisely due to the curved shape, but 0.1~0.2mm has worn off from either guide rib
# The side ribs have also *worn considerably wider*, allowing the battery more freedom to twist slightly in the tower, which *I think is the largest factor why this battery works*, while the unworn ones do not.

!image-20250724-141730.png|width=834,height=662,alt="image-20250724-141730.png"!

I took this battery back to Tallinn to measure it better and try to find the exact dimensions we would need to acheive on the C3 housing so the battery would not stick ☝️ 



*NEXT STEPS:*

* Try to find a frame that sticks the same way as the ones I tested in Riga. I will try the brand new frames in HQ first and if none of those stick, we need to find a test subject in TLN WH.
* Use that frame to see why exactly the worn-in battery works better and measure how much and where the C3.1 housing must be changed to work as well as the worn-in one from the first day.
* Need to make a decision and create an SOP how to mitigate the problem with the first 20k batch of C3 batteries before the C3 launches in new markets. 
** Best bet currently seems using the belt grinder (as WHs already have it) and just sand down the frames one-by-one that come back to WH with a stuck battery. 
** ⚠️ However we must figure out a method for mechanics to reliably test and find the root cause before going wild with the sander, as not all frames are equal and on some frames the problem is elsewhere.



*ADDITIONAL:*

!image-20250724-142345.png|width=1070,height=706,alt="image-20250724-142345.png"!

Almost all C3 batteries in Riga also had rubbing marks in these corners. It seems that the width of the lock plate on the tower is also slightly varying frame to frame and some frames also stick there. However I am sure that this is not a major issue and does not need addressing for the first 20k C3 batteries.

h2. Initial Analysis

This issue arises in scenarios where the APM (Alternative Payment Method) under-captures funds. Below is the sequence of events that leads to this bug:

* A user books a ride using an APM payment method.
* The ride is subsequently canceled for various reasons, and the user incurs a cancellation fee.
* This cancellation fee is lower than the ride amount, resulting in a captured amount that is less than the authorized amount.
* For APMs, this lower captured amount during booking triggers a partial refund operation, causing the payment status to transition from captured to partially refunded (see example: [3473818198|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/commerce-payment/payments/3473818198]).
* When a full refund request is received for the corresponding booking, a new full refund task is created [here|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/platform/commerce/balance_user/main/service/strategy/full_refund/FullRefundStrategyBase.ts#L116].
* Upon execution of this task, a refund request is made for the entire amount specified on the PSP payment method [here|https://github.com/bolteu/bolt-server/blob/develop/src/platform/commerce/balance_user/main/service/strategy/full_refund/FullRefundSingleStrategy.ts#L144].
* However, this amount exceeds the remaining balance available for refund on the payment method, leading to the rejection of the refund transaction. +*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt recently terminated a fleet driver (Ihab Abdullah Fathi) due to multiple incidents of harassment.
** 31 May 2024: A passenger reported that the driver made sexual advances toward her and suggested coming with her to her apartment.
** 3 July 2024: A passenger stated that the driver called her attractive and asked her to give him her phone number.
** 6 January 2025: A passenger reported that the driver inappropriately touched her breast and behaved disrespectfully overall.
** 29 June 2025: A passenger reported that she was harassed and physically touched by the driver.
* On 17 July, fleet reached out requesting information about the incidents (see letter).
** Fleet has flagged that the driver is beyond his probationary period. As such, fleet expects that their termination of the driver will result in a wrongful termination lawsuit. Fleet wants evidence to be able to properly defend itself if this happens.
** Fleet as requested the following details:
*** *_1. Time of the incident_*
*** *_2. Name and address of the customer (as a witness in court)_*
*** *_3. Precise description of the incident: What happened, when, how, and who was involved? Are there any other witnesses?_*
*** *_4. Time and nature of the complaint received_*
*** *_5. Scope and content of the internal investigation, as well as possible witnesses in court_*
*** *_6. Recordings of conversations with drivers and customers_*
** Fleet recognises GDPR, but looks to “mutual contractual relationship” as creating a duty of information.
* *Request*: What information can we share with the fleet?

+*THOUGHTS*+

* This is not a DSAR submitted on a driver’s behalf - _very_ unlikely that the driver would consent to sharing this information. As such, we must treat this as a third-party request.
* Analysis:
** *(1) Is the identity of the fleet verified?*
*** {color:#4c9aff}TBC with the requestor.{color}
** *(2) Is there a legal basis for sharing?*
*** There will not be a legal basis _compelling_ Bolt to share this data. As such, we would need to rely on legitimate interest.
*** EDPB [Guidance|https://www.edpb.europa.eu/system/files/2024-10/edpb_guidelines_202401_legitimateinterest_en.pdf] on legitimate interest hints at civil proceedings being a good reason for sharing data with an involved third party. As such, we could argue that Bolt has a legitimate interest here, particularly given the litigation context.
** *(3) Is the data being requested proportionate?*
*** 1. {color:#36b37e}*Yes*{color}. Not overly intrusive. Proportionate and necessary to the fleet’s defence.
*** 2. {color:#ff5630}*No*{color}. Overly intrusive, third-party data, and outside of the expectations of the customer that submitted the complaint. Without a litigation having actually commenced, we could only really share this in a justifiable way with the customer’s consent. We would need a court order to share more.
*** 3. {color:#36b37e}*Yes*{color}, albeit partially (i.e., in a way that does not identify the passenger, for the reasons set out above). We would need a court order to share more.
*** 4. See above.
*** 5. Can share {color:#36b37e}*some details of internal investigation*{color}, but not {color:#ff5630}*employee details*{color} (for the reasons set out above). We would need a court order to share more.
*** 6. {color:#ff5630}*No*{color}. Recordings do not exist, and conversations may have been deleted due to retention periods. In any case, sharing conversations likely to be regarded as intrusive. We would need a court order to share more.
* Conclusion:
** *_If we can verify the request, we can rely on legitimate interest to share the date / time of the incidents, a high-level description of the incidents and a high-level description of the internal investigation in each case. To share any more, we would need either consent or a court order to protect our position, given balancing exercise._*
*** Probably best to share this in a format that we have specifically created.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** Are we confident of the fleet’s identity?
** What information does the fleet have access to already?
** Please send links of the relevant complaints, the driver’s profile,  the fleet’s profile and internal investigation notes.
* Advise the business to produce a summary in table format, which privacy can review and redact. I can then also draft a response.

* We need to reassess the full refund process to implement a proper fix for this issue.
* As an interim solution, we can introduce additional validations within the booking service.

Hi Egle,



In April we launched a 4 week pilot of dynamic commission for drivers in Helsinki. We decided to only invest in certain rides by reducing the commission rate. No communication to drivers. The test proceeded smoothly, and the results were good.

Then, last month we did a second test with dynamic pricing for riders. To ensure that driver earnings remained unaffected, we continued using dynamic commission --> when rider prices dropped, we lowered the commission; when prices rose, we increased it. On average, the drivers maintained a  25% commission. We did not inform drivers or riders about this test. Only after drivers began contacting support with questions, we shared an explanation outlining how the test functioned.

For reference:
Standard commission in Helsinki: 25%
Dynamic commission range: 15–35%



The end goal with these tests are to convert more searches into rides and with that improve efficiency on the platform. Both tests have now ended, but we have not yet made a decision on whether to roll out these features permanently.

Let me know if you want me to clarify anything.

Together with [~accountid:712020:62c58726-d2a7-4caa-b649-ec7bd1c6a2ff] we find out, that for now the best would be to:

1. Utilise daily Crowdin API reports (pt-accuracy) which serves info about AI pre-translated queries, number of approved queries without edition, and weightUnits, which is Crowdin way of calculating accuracy of precalculation (word approved without editions gives 1, while words edited, depending on the distance, numbers between 0 and 1.) 

2. Track dates of our updates into prompts for a particular project and language. It will allow us to track when we actually have new version of the prompt and when we should start expect changes in accuracy. 

A combination of these two should give us an understanding of how our AI translations are performing.

Just for the reference, what we considered during this process (I’m copy pasting with small editions my summary from chat with Heiti) : 

# Our goal is to find how many strings pre-translated by AI are approved and how many of them are edited, and what the average distance of edition is. This is to give us an understanding of our prompt/model quality on the project and language level.
# Prompts are generated per project per language
# Currently, prompts are updated and overwritten in Crowdin, so we need to keep track of dates of changes, because in Crowdin one prompt ID serves multiple languages and we can't distinguish in other way, but this is a separate problem from distance measuring.
# Full scan of all strings every day seems to be an overkill. There is a 20 calls per second limit in the Crowdin APP, which allows for max 1.7 million calls per 24h. And we already have more than 2m words. 
# There is an option to use CroQL to filter for strings pre-translated by AI and scan only them, but eventually, I would expect 100% of data to be translated with AI, so it needs full scan.
# There is some potential in webhook events, as we can track events of editing pre-translated strings -> I don't know if this serves two strings to compare to get distance
# There is an option of programmatically creating prompts in Crowdin, which would help with distinguishing between languages, but this is a separate problem from distance measuring.
# The AI API also has some reports to be generated, but they are only about tokens used.

# Done for both tickets, the current one and [this one|https://taxify.atlassian.net/browse/LSS-53693].
# My understanding is that this case, as well as the other one, have already been resolved. However*,* ANPC has requested general clarifications regarding the way Bolt operates, particularly in relation to the roles and responsibilities of Delivery Partners (Bolt Food) and Drivers (Bolt Rides). As a next step, I propose to prepare two standard explanatory templates:
(i) *one for Bolt Food*, and
(ii) *one for Rides*, which would outline the general commercial framework, including aspects such as contractual relationships, liability, professional independence etc.
# In terms of improvement areas, it's worth noting that both complaints appear to have been triggered by *automated processes within the Bolt platforms*:

* In the Bolt Food case, the customer's refund request was automatically rejected due to a negative refund score, which prevented the automated refund mechanism from functioning (although the customer never received the order so he was entitled to the refund regardless of the negative score);
* In the Rides case, the fare increased significantly (more than double) after the customer changed the destination three times, as a result of an automated pricing mechanism.

In both instances, ANPC considered that such automatic outcomes do not reflect fair treatment of the consumer and could be seen as infringing upon the economic interests of the customer.

What could be improved in my opinion:

* An automatic trigger should be implemented for *manual review* in cases where a refund is denied solely due to the customer's negative refund score. In such instances, a human agent should assess whether the customer is, in fact, entitled to a refund based on the specific circumstances of the request;
* Include or improve *real-time explanations in the app* (e.g., “This refund was denied due to repeated prior claims”; "Due to multiple destination changes, dynamic pricing rules apply");
* Be able to explain to consumer/ANPC *the underlying logic and criteria used in automated decision-making processes*.

Please let me know your thoughts on the above.

Thank you!

Specifically, for us to process your request and release sensitive or confidential information, the PDF document must be formally authenticated and clearly state the *legal basis* that authorizes us to share the requested information with your authority.

This means it needs to be either:

* *Digitally signed:* Utilizing a verifiable digital signature that confirms the sender's identity and the document's integrity.
* *A scanned copy of a physically signed and officially stamped document:* This is the traditional method for official requests, bearing the officer's *wet signature* and *official department stamp*.

These requirements are critical for several reasons, including:

* *Verifying the authenticity and authority of the request:* Ensuring it genuinely originates from an authorized law enforcement or government entity.

* *Maintaining proper legal and audit records:* For accountability and to demonstrate due diligence in handling sensitive data.
* *Protecting our company and our customers:* By ensuring information is only released under legally sound and verifiable circumstances.

We want to clarify that while a *Production Order* is always a perfectly valid and recognized legal instrument for compelling information, it is not an ultimate requirement for _every_ type of information request. Please provide a revised PDF document that includes either a valid digital signature or a clear scan of the physically signed and stamped original, *and explicitly states the legal basis for your request.*

Hi [~accountid:63fdee79feb4b150c57651b4], just following up on this - please see below a summary of ISS' comments and the implications: 

+*Clause 3 (Termination)*+

→ _Summary of our changes to this clause/ISS' response_ 

we initially sought to amend clause 3.2(a) so that +either party+ can terminate the agreement on 3 months' notice, giving Bolt the flexibility to ‘get out’ of the agreement if the deal becomes commercially unviable or too high-risk. *ISS have rejected this* and are only willing to allow themselves the right to terminate for convenience - meaning *Bolt is locked into the agreement unless ISS breaches the agreement.* 

→ _What are the implications of this?_

* ISS can walk away at any time with 3 months' notice, for any reason. 
* We can’t exist unless ISS commits a material breach (i.e. fails to pay). As mentioned above, if the deal becomes unprofitable or too operationally burdensome, we’re stuck. 
* we carry rebate liabilities and monthly reporting burdens under the agreement - if our margins deteriorate or the workload increases, we have no route to exit without breaching. 

→ _Next steps_

* Please confirm whether you would like me to: 
** push back on this clause and propose some wording; or
** whether you are comfortable with the above risks.  

+*Clause 7.2 (Invoicing and Payment)*+ 

→ _Summary of our changes to this clause/ISS' response_ 

* The original drafting of this clause meant that Bolt would still be required to continue paying rebates if ISS disputed a rebate. Our change here proposed that, if ISS disputes a rebate, we wouldn’t have to pay the disputed portion until resolved. 
* ISS have pushed back - they want to avoid any suspension of payment obligations and are only willing to agree the the parties “negotiate in good faith”.

→ _Next steps_

* You will see from the redline amendments and my response to ISS that I have proposed a compromise clause that allows both parties to enter into good faith negotiations where there is a dispute, but allows us to withhold disputed amounts whilst there is a dispute. 

+*Clause 9.2 (ISS Group Members' Rights)*+ 

→ _Summary of our changes to this clause/ISS' response_ 

* I originally struck this clause out because ISS group members (that are not party to this agreement) can enforce benefits under this agreement (i.e. an entity that is part of the ISS group, but is not *ISS Ireland Limited* can issue claims or queries against/to Bolt. 
* If we are only contracting with ISS Ireland Limited, I suggest that this clause is deleted so that we avoid exposure to indirect enforcement rights. 
* You will see that I have responded to ISS' query within the document on this point. 

+Next Steps+ 

Attached is the latest version where I have (a) accepted any changes that ISS have not objected to, (b) responded to ISS' comments and (c) inserted placeholders for the date of the agreement and the Effective Date of the agreement to be inserted. *Note: please either insert the Effective Date or, if ISS will insert the Effective Date, that the date is correct and as agreed.* 

*Please confirm:* 

(a) how you would like me to proceed with clause 3 as flagged above and I will update the agreement accordingly;

(b) whether you agree with my approach/responses to ISS on clauses to clauses 7.2 and 9.2 (or whether you are comfortable with the risks associated with the original wording and are happy to accept ISS' original clauses); and

(c) that Finance has approved this rebate agreement. 

Best wishes

Detailed status:

*** 40% discount -> 0.18, rounded to 0.2
*** 50% discount -> 0.15, rounded to 0.2

At this stage, we still don’t understand what specific risks PH believes it faces, or why our proposed mutual protections are not acceptable.

*NDA – Article 5 (p. 1 and 3):*

* We proposed standard mutual liability protections to reflect balanced, industry-standard NDA practice.
* PH insists on making only the _Receiving Party_ fully liable — this makes the agreement effectively one-sided, despite being labeled “mutual.”
* We cannot accept full liability for indirect or negligent acts of affiliates or employees that are beyond our direct control. It undermines the core principle of a mutual NDA. In practice, it means PH has all the protection and none of the accountability, while Bolt takes all the risk.
* We suggest limiting liability to unauthorized disclosures caused by gross negligence or willful misconduct, which still offers PH strong protection.

Please ask PH to explain:

* What specific risks or harm they are concerned about if this clause is balanced?
* What examples do they have of a case where a mutual clause like ours would fail to protect them?



*General and Special Terms:*
We understand that PH continues to request a separate main agreement and does not recognize the current structure of General Terms and Special Terms as a complete contractual framework.

* What specific difference or legal effect does PH see between a structure that uses a standalone agreement with annexes versus the current setup where the General Terms and Special Terms together form the full Agreement?
* Are there particular legal or commercial risks that PH is trying to mitigate by requesting a main contract document?
* Is there a precedent or internal requirement driving this request?



Please explain to the customer that *Clause 6.3* in the General Terms does _not_ impact their legal right to bring claims within the statutory 3-year period under Azerbaijani law. The clause only sets a financial cap on Bolt’s total liability — based on payments made in the 3 months before the first claim — which is standard practice for SaaS platforms like Bolt that act as intermediaries.
This cap ensures liability is proportional to actual usage and helps maintain predictability. It does _not_ waive or reduce their right to claim.
If this remains a blocker, we can explore extending the reference period to 6 or 12 months, or even offering a fixed monetary cap — but this requires RSM approval.



*Clause 6.4* in the General Terms -  We do not directly control the actions of independent service providers (such as drivers), and therefore cannot assume full liability for their conduct or for consequential damages beyond our control. This approach is standard for platforms like ours.
Could you please clarify with the client, what specific risk or scenario is PH trying to mitigate by asking for the removal of this clause?

Thanks [~accountid:712020:27f468e3-5ccd-433f-9a22-f38e71d9b717] - I have reviewed and my thoughts are below. In short, we have a legal basis to share most of the requested information with the fleet owner, provided that: (1) we have *_verified the identity_* of the requestor; and (2) the data being requested is *_proportionate_*.

In practice, point (2) means that we can disclose the data provided that it does not including anything that could be used to identify third parties (e.g., passengers, Bolt employees etc.). Breaking this down per request, we can share the following categories of data in the first instance:

# *Time of the incident:* {color:#36b37e}Yes{color}.
# *Name / address of passenger*: {color:#ff5630}No{color}.
# *Precise description*: {color:#36b37e}Yes{color}, provided that we remove anything that could link the trip to a specific passenger.
# *Time / nature of complaint*: See above.
# *Scope / content of internal investigation, and witnesses:* We can share a {color:#36b37e}high-level overview of internal notes{color} made about the complaint. We should not, however, share the {color:#ff5630}names / identities of Bolt employees{color} involved in the decision.
# *Recordings of conversations*: We do not _record_ conversations between drivers and passengers. We also should not share {color:#ff5630}messages between drivers and passengers{color} in the first instance, as this is quite intrusive.

{panel:bgColor=#deebff}
*NEXT STEPS:*

# Please double-check that we are comfortable that the person making the request is indeed the owner of the fleet (i.e., that the contact details / names match up), and that their story holds up (i.e., that the driver they are asking about is under their fleet, and that driver was indeed suspended).
# Please then compile (in a table format) the date / time of each incident, together with a description of the incident (removing anything that could be used to identify the passenger(s)) and extracts of any internal notes made on the case.
# I would then be happy to review the data, apply any additional redactions as needed, and prepare a response.
# Once the data / response are finalised, we can send them to the fleet.
{panel}

Happy to discuss if you have any questions 🙂

* [DEX Data EDA|https://taxify.atlassian.net/wiki/x/OIEXigE]: Had a meeting with Zhenyu last week to discuss initial EDA and we agreed on a proper methodology. The methodology and main results are available in the document. 
* *Final Remarks on the Analysis:*
** Strong signal for rider re-activations, clean signal in a good number of cities
** Uplift for new rider activations is usually quite small, bad signal in most cities - my suggestion is to drop modeling incrementality here as impact is rather small, we can model the total new activations as a time series 
** Let’s use weekly campaigns as source of incrementality for now, but DEX data is very promising and we should push for more coverage across LTO cities and more frequency on those experiments (can be quite relevant for noisier metrics like sessions / active rider)
** Once we have incrementality for rider churn figured out we can combine both components into a larger model to estimate active riders, I propose a quick backtest compared to current model to see if we lose a lot of accuracy.

*Next steps:*

* I’ll write a brief document summarizing this whole analysis next week
* Priority for next couple of weeks will be looking into rider churn incrementality

Hi [~accountid:5e343bd0a834270cb09975d0],

From a Legal perspective, there *do not appear to be any specific UK legal restrictions* preventing payments into business bank accounts for self-employed drivers. That said, there are some *important legal and compliance risks* to be aware of:

* *Verification and Ownership*: It's generally harder to verify that a business bank account belongs to the driver in question. While Bolt isn’t an AML/KYC-regulated entity in the UK, we should still assess whether our current identity verification processes are sufficient to prevent fraud, misdirected payments, or misuse of third-party company accounts.
* *DAC7 Risk Alignment*: As [~accountid:712020:726e5ea0-027c-4c31-a0fd-2c23b80dc56c] noted, using business accounts may raise DAC7 reporting complexity. If payments are routed to corporate entities, Legal’s concern is whether Bolt can reliably identify the *true beneficial recipient* of income. HMRC may scrutinize arrangements that obscure income flows and could allege facilitation of tax evasion or DAC7 breaches if controls are weak.
* *Employment Law Considerations*: If an individual sets up a company to receive income and only drives for Bolt, HMRC may take the view that IR35/off-payroll working rules apply. This could raise employment law and tax exposure for Bolt, especially if it appears the arrangement is being used to circumvent worker protections.

In summary, while there’s *no direct legal prohibition*, introducing business accounts may increase *legal, tax and reputational risk* unless mitigated by stricter onboarding and monitoring procedures. This question is ultimately a business/Finance decision and we recommend Ops collaborates closely with Finance to assess whether existing checks are sufficient, or whether additional controls are needed. 

Best wishes

Thank you [~accountid:712020:726e5ea0-027c-4c31-a0fd-2c23b80dc56c] for your feedback. 

[~accountid:614ad8fe76e34d006967d6bd], just to confirm the position from a legal perspective, there are no express Irish legal restrictions preventing us from paying drivers into business bank accounts. However, there are a few *key risks to flag*:

* *Ownership verification*: Business accounts can obscure the identity of the driver receiving payment. While Bolt isn’t subject to AML/KYC rules in Ireland, we may need to enhance our internal verification standards to avoid fraud, payment disputes, or scrutiny from Revenue.
* *DAC7 reporting*: As per [~accountid:712020:726e5ea0-027c-4c31-a0fd-2c23b80dc56c]'s comments, payments to companies must be reported differently, and Irish Revenue is taking a firm approach to platform compliance. If we don’t collect company registration and beneficial ownership details, Bolt may be exposed to enforcement under DAC7.
* *Employment status risk*: If a driver routes income through a company but works solely for Bolt, regulators may view this as an attempt to sidestep employment obligations - potentially triggering worker classification challenges and tax risk.

In summary, while legally permissible, allowing business accounts in Ireland increases exposure on several fronts. Any policy change should be paired with tighter onboarding and compliance checks, and we’d recommend alignment with Finance before proceeding.

Best wishes

Hey [~accountid:712020:338dfd87-ef5d-40bb-b10d-871b880aa66d] !

From a practical side, I think we should  have two separate agreements: 

# Bolt’s standard contract, which each party would sign separately (e.g. via salesforce, so it shouldn’t be too much hassle).
# A separate marketing agreement (under which they get the 20k), signed by all parties together. 

I think the separate agreements for the standard contract are necessary for 1. accounting purposes (I assume from a practical perspective, all “normal” payments still need to go to different legal entities), and 2. practical purposes - should any legal claims arise in relation to one of the restos, we want to have the possibility to terminate only the one legal entity from our platform. 

But for the 20k payment,  I guess it makes sense to have a separate agreement for this, since I assume their obligations are tied to the other restos/ they would be jointly liable (usually  the restaurants have a co-financing obligation, e.g. we put in 20k, they also have to invest in marketing; or have to meet certain KPIs)? So from that side, i think it would make sense they are under one contact, so if one restaurant/legal entity breaches, then we have a right to withdraw/ask back the 20k from others as well? But ofc this depends on the set-up, I’m not sure I understand how they want it to work from the practical side. 

But overall, for the standard contract, as far as I remember, we have not really signed any agreements where we would have several parties sign the same agreement.

Hello [~accountid:626a69abb31e6f0068634a56] the commission should be the same for all orders in KFC’s case in RO, which is 16.06%.

The idea is that KFC and their HQ are aware that a delivery platform’s commission includes 2 sides: they are paying part of the commission for the marketplace (basically to be allowed to be part of our partners selection) and the 2nd part is for delivery (to have their orders delivered with our couriers). As you may know there are also restaurants that do their own delivery and in that case the commission we take is lower because they are delivering the orders on their own cost.

KFC has this setup for Glovo and Wolt, our competitors in Romania, and they say that they have 16% commission which is split in 5% commission for marketplace and 11% commission for delivery. This is shown in the weekly report they have there on 2 separate columns, with one amount representing the total commission taken from them in the last week for marketplace (which is 5% of sales in their case) and the total commission taken for delivery (which is 11%).

As far as I know, at least in admin, we do not have 2 separate fields to highlight the marketplace commission and the delivery commission, we can only see the total commission which is 16.06% and I have no idea if somewhere else this split is highlighted or not. 

Keep in mind that just because on Glovo & Wolt the split is 5% marketplace & 11% delivery does not mean that it should be the same on Bolt Food.

This request is with high urgency on KFC’s part because they will have an audit at the beginning of august and they need to have the weekly report tailored this way until then. 

Let me know if any additional info are required from my side. I can ask KFC to offer an example of weekly report from competition if you need to get a clearer idea of how it should look.

Thanks!

h3. Launch Model Overview

* Built to solve campaign spend optimisation challenges from Canada launch
** Started spending 70% of GMV on campaigns
** Took too long to realise supply spend could be reduced
** *Model aims to signal optimal spend levels beforehand*
* Two-sided marketplace approach comparing value propositions
** Rider value prop: net price (actual price minus demand spend impact) vs competition
** Driver value prop: earnings per trip vs competition, not earnings per hour due to liquidity disadvantage
** Must account for ETA differences - if 8 minutes longer wait time, need to be significantly cheaper
* Uses regression models for price/ETA relationships and demand elasticity
** Built from scratch, not based on London scaling sandbox
** Price vs conversion rates and ETA vs conversion rates analysis
** Manual localization assumptions needed for different market behaviors

h3. Current Model Mechanics & Pain Points

* Forecasting approach uses last 2 weeks average for baseline metrics
** Online hours, rider activation, rider churn, rides per rider
** Have to provides manual input for online hours due to driver registration funnel control
* Spend impact calculation biggest challenge without proper A/B tests
** Current assumptions: online hours less sensitive (1:0.5 relationship), riders more sensitive (1:1)
** Massimo launched weekly demand campaign experiments for discount vs active user cost ratio
** Need curves for different spend levels vs metrics like rides per rider
** Supply side still lacks data - no A/B tests launched yet
* Regional vs global curves discussion
** Should be localised but need data from big markets first
** Asian vs European playbooks likely will be different. But let’s start with the global 🙂 - Small towns may need global proxy initially, improve accuracy over time

h3. Next Steps

* Kateryna to replicate model in Databricks notebook
** Start with last week values replication
** Build exit scenario (no spend changes)
** Add spending impact relationships
** Implement rider/driver value prop comparisons
* Regular sync meetings needed (weekly or biweekly) given model complexity

* Weekly campaigns (aggregated by week)
* ATE is given by: (Treatment Enrollments * (Treatment Active Riders / Treatment Enrollments - Control Active Riders / Control Enrollments)) / Previous Week’s Total Active Riders
* Interpretation of ATE: % active riders uplift on treatment vs control
* We measure the ATE by the % of GMV that is spent on demand incentives for the churning cohorts 



In cities where we have a good history of weekly incentives campaigns, the signal is relatively strong, being highly correlated with spend. The level of churn reduction is also not insignificant, reaching around 1.5-2% of total active riders on average for higher levels of spend.

Nous accusons réception de vos messages des 13 et 14 juillet 2025 concernant votre statut d’indépendant, le traitement de votre taux d’annulation et les conditions de rémunération liées aux courses annulées par les clients. Nous vous remercions pour votre franchise et souhaitons, par la présente, vous apporter une réponse juridique complète et transparente.

h4. 1. Concernant *votre statut d’indépendant*

Nous vous confirmons que vous intervenez en tant que prestataire de services indépendant, conformément au cadre contractuel qui vous lie à Bolt.

Les Conditions Générales d’Utilisation stipulent expressément (article 10.4) :

_« [...] la relation entre les parties ne constitue pas un contrat de travail, et ne crée aucun lien de subordination entre le Prestataire et Bolt. »_

Vous conservez une pleine liberté dans l’organisation de votre activité, notamment en ce qui concerne vos horaires et la sélection des courses. Comme vous le savez, et comme rappelé à l’article 4.6, vous conservez une pleine liberté dans l’organisation de votre activité, notamment en ce qui concerne vos horaires et la sélection des courses :

_« Le Chauffeur a la possibilité d'accepter, de refuser ou d'ignorer des demandes de Clients [...] à sa convenance et sans conséquence sur le maintien du présent Contrat. »_

Bolt agit uniquement en tant que centrale de mise en relation et ne fournit pas les services de transport eux-mêmes (article 10.3).

h4. 2. *Concernant le taux d’annulation*

Le suivi de certaines données d’activité, comme le taux d’annulation, n’a pas vocation à restreindre votre indépendance. En revanche, comme tout service d’intermédiation numérique, Bolt se doit d’assurer une qualité et une continuité de service pour l’ensemble des utilisateurs.

Certaines pratiques sont donc encadrées lorsqu’elles portent atteinte au bon fonctionnement de la plateforme. L’article 11.3.1 interdit, par exemple, les annulations excessives après acceptation d’une course, non pas pour limiter vos refus, mais pour prévenir des comportements désorganisant la mise en relation :

_« [...] en annulant de manière excessive des services de transport à la demande après avoir indiqué votre volonté de les fournir. »_

Ce dispositif est prévu par le règlement européen (UE) 2022/2065 dit « Digital Services Act (DSA), qui impose aux plateformes en ligne comme Bolt de mettre en place des règles transparentes, non discriminatoires et proportionnées afin de garantir un fonctionnement équitable. Cela implique que toute mesure d’équilibrage (comme la gestion des taux d’annulation) doit reposer sur des critères objectifs, accessibles, et contestables.

Nous nous conformons à ces exigences et vous pouvez, si besoin, faire valoir vos observations via notre [Système Interne de Traitement des Plaintes|https://bolt.eu/fr-fr/legal/tnc-internal-rules/?category=rides], prévu à l’article 14.6.

h4. 3. *Sur la rémunération en cas d’annulation par un client*

Lorsque le client annule une course au-delà du délai prévu dans l’application, vous pouvez bénéficier d’une compensation (article 4.14) :

_« [...] le Prestataire a droit à une partie du Prix pour les Services de transport annulés (tel que communiqué au Chauffeur). »_

Nous vous rappelons que l'application indique, à chaque annulation, si des frais sont dus. Si vous estimez qu’une indemnité n’a pas été appliquée à tort, vous pouvez soumettre une demande via l’outil de révision du prix, dans un délai de 24 heures (article 4.13).

Enfin, nous vous prions de noter que Bolt respecte strictement vos droits en tant que travailleur indépendant et s’efforce d’appliquer un cadre équilibré, conforme aux exigences du droit français et européen. Si vous souhaitez faire valoir certains éléments ou demander des ajustements, nous vous invitons à utiliser le système prévu à cet effet, accessible [ici|https://bolt.eu/fr-fr/legal/tnc-internal-rules/?category=rides].

Nous vous remercions pour votre engagement sur la plateforme et restons à votre disposition pour toute clarification complémentaire.

Veuillez recevoir, Monsieur, nos salutations distinguées.

*Drive Safety: Driving Score*Hey team! Super excited to share that our [*Driving Score*|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TI7BJJuYqcHq6Fbdu6z_sDlmpWbFo0geO0ZcTMirvsQ/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.mtkno8ygwxgb] feature is now launched in A/B test!

*What it does:*
We now calculate and communicate a *driving score* after every ride, based on: *speeding* and *harsh driving behavior*.

*Why this matters:*
Speeding and reckless driving account for *~28% of damage costs*. Looking at parallel services and our damage costs, we can project *cost savings of 1.5% of GMV* with such a system.

*How users see it:*

* A numeric *driving score* in their *score overview page*
* *Score for each drive* in score history page
* *FAQ section* to explain how it works

*Launch plan:*

# Public A/B test 1 - EE LT
## Experiment starts with 40% of users, gradually increasing to 100%
## *Treatment* (half of enrolled users): Score calculated and visible
## *Control* (other half of enrolled users): Score calculated but not visible
# Public A/B test 2 - LV CZ
## Same setup as test 1

[Full launch plans and timelines here|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1TI7BJJuYqcHq6Fbdu6z_sDlmpWbFo0geO0ZcTMirvsQ/edit?tab=t.0#heading=h.av0isnnw9239]
Note: DE is excluded from first rollout due to IoT mounting issues. The feature will be rolled out there once the fleet rotation is completed by Autumn.

* Continuous ad-hoc improvements based on user feedback
* Include a first incentive to encourage score improvement

Given the limitations mentioned above → namely no support for re-randomisation, we will redefine our approach.  

Problem : Given the limitations of not having re-randomisation in the test we will need to redefine our approach. 

* *Solution 1:* Still try to replicate the same approach with multiple tests. 
** *How -* Have 3 separate tests Month 1, Month 2, Month 3 and we know this will ensure re-randomisation each month. 
*** Test 1 starts on 1st of January and ends on 31st of Jan. 
*** Test 2 starts on 1st of february and ends on 28th of feb and so on. 
** *Problem to solve:* if we keep weekly enrolment that would mean that company that is enrolled at the end of Test 1 (let’s say only 7 days left), will also be enrolled in the beginning of test 2. Which we want to avoid: 1) Holdouts? 2) how does enrolment expiry work exactly - if two tests have the same comms only campaign - does it say target already enrolled or that works only for campaigns?
* *Solution 2:* modify looker enrolments of companies in a way that pretty much takes care of the problem from above. Very tricky since there are different enrolments happening mostly on the LCM side. 
* *Solution 3:* similar approach but instead of weekly enrolments we do monthly
** This way we don’t have the problem described above. And analysis can be similar to before -> where “we call it session based analysis” 
* Another layer could be -> countries with higher stability can be quarterly and countries with lower stability MoM in terms of results kept at monthly.


So far this is the thinking right now - > will update later on decision

Hi, [~accountid:5f5b93718d3ae70076d6b271] , 

If our investigation confirms that the scooter’s brakes malfunctioned, this may indicate a fault in our service. In such a case, the user may be eligible to claim compensation *only in the event of permanent disability or death*, as covered by the Personal Accident Insurance included in our service. Therefore, your observation is correct, *our insurance policy does not extend to personal property damage*.

However, under +the Romanian Civil Code+, compensation for property damage may be considered if *fault is established* and the user proves a *direct causal link* between our (_alleged_) service failure and their loss.

Furthermore, according to +Law no. 240/2004 on product liability+, Bolt may be liable for the damaged headphones only if:

* The item was used for *personal (non-commercial)* purposes;
* The *value of the item exceeds RON 200*;
* The damage is directly linked to a defect in the product we provided.



We suggest replying to ANPC with a clear explanation of the following:

# *The outcome of our technical inspection*, if completed, only if it favors us.
# *The scope of insurance coverage*, which is limited to bodily injury (permanent disability or death).
# *Our Terms of Service limitation* on property damage compensation.
# *Our willingness to assess compensation* for the headphones only if the user demonstrates that:
#* The item was for personal use;
#* The value exceeds *RON 200*;
#* There is a *direct causal link* between the alleged service fault and the damage.

CASE WHEN i.profile_features__user__user_spending_profile = 'trusted good spender' THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS trusted_spender_logic,
CASE WHEN (i.user_payments__successful_payments_trusted > 0 AND SUM(i.user_payments__chargeback_payments + i.user_payments__payment_problems) = 0) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS trusted_payments_logic,
CASE WHEN (i.card_info__challenge__add_card__liability_shift = 'with_friction' OR (i.card_info__challenge__payment__days_since_liability_shift_with_friction IS NOT NULL AND i.card_info__challenge__payment__days_since_liability_shift_with_friction >= 0 AND i.card_info__challenge__payment__days_since_liability_shift_with_friction < 30)) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS passed_theeds_logic,
CASE WHEN (i.profile_features__user__user_spending_profile = 'trusted good spender' OR (i.user_payments__successful_payments_trusted > 0 AND SUM(i.user_payments__chargeback_payments + i.user_payments__payment_problems) = 0) OR (i.card_info__challenge__add_card__liability_shift = 'with_friction' OR (i.card_info__challenge__payment__days_since_liability_shift_with_friction IS NOT NULL AND i.card_info__challenge__payment__days_since_liability_shift_with_friction >= 0 AND i.card_info__challenge__payment__days_since_liability_shift_with_friction < 30))) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END AS combined_logic,
APPROX_DISTINCT(i.id,0.0041) AS count_checks,
APPROX_DISTINCT(i.user_id,0.0041) AS count_users,
APPROX_DISTINCT(co.id,0.0041) AS count_orders,
ROUND(SUM(co.partner_price_eur),2) AS sum_partner_price_eur,
ROUND(SUM(co.user_price_eur),2) AS sum_user_price_eur,
ROUND(SUM(co.potential_fraud_loss_eur),2) AS sum_potential_fraud_loss_eur,
ROUND(SUM(CASE WHEN (co.is_initial_chargeback OR co.is_payment_problem OR co.propagated_chargeback) THEN co.potential_fraud_loss_eur ELSE 0 END),2) AS sum_potential_fraud_loss_eur_cb_related
FROM ng_pii.etl_user_order_request i
LEFT JOIN ng_public.etl_denormalized_commerce_orders co ON co.fraud_calculation_id = i.id AND co.order_type = 'rides' AND co.created_date >= date '2025-05-01'
WHERE i.created_date >= date '2025-05-01'
AND i.order_country = 'th'
AND i.decision = 'challenge'
AND i.card_info__card_issuer LIKE 'REVOLUT%'
GROUP BY 1,2,4,i.user_payments__successful_payments_trusted,i.card_info__challenge__add_card__liability_shift,i.profile_features__user__user_spending_profile,i.card_info__challenge__payment__days_since_liability_shift_with_friction
ORDER BY 1 DESC{code}

{quote}The elapsed wall time when TiDB Coprocessor executor waiting all Coprocessor requests to finish (note: when there are JOIN in SQL statement, multiple TiDB Coprocessor executors may be running in parallel, which may cause this time not being a wall time) {quote}

{quote}The {{Coprocessor Executor Time}} bucket is the time TiDB spends *after* it has received the raw KV/coprocessor batches from TiKV but *before* the final result is sent back to the client. Concretely that means:

# Pulling in the streamed/chunked results that came over GRPC from TiKV
# De‐serializing (decoding) those byte‐streams into TiDB’s in‐memory {{chunk.Chunk}} objects
# Pushing those Chunks through TiDB’s local (vectorized) executor operators – for example:
• applying any filters or projections that didn’t or couldn’t get fully pushed down to TiKV
• merging or finishing partial aggregates
• doing topN/OrderBy/Limit on the merged stream
• building or probing hash tables for joins (if you’re in a local hash‐join rather than a coprocessor pushdown join)
# Producing the final row stream (again in chunks) that TiDB then hands to its network layer to return to your client{quote}

[~accountid:6130627ef0bf520069526076] adjusted the jig. It needs one more slight adjustment and then it is good to go. 

It seems that for production we have to CNC the jig from aluminum or get it laser cut from steel. The 3D-print is too soft and can not be used to hold down the cable anchor while tightening the bolt, it will deform easily. While it is fine to also tighten as a separate operation, but it can save on assembly time if we can do it in a single operation.

The bike is set up and can be tested. Brake feels OK and braking power is really good. The lever is slightly mushy, which I think is a combination of the roller brake design, our brake levers design and cheap cable housings. As the brake is powerful there is no need to grab it too hard and the slight mushy feeling does not bother while riding.

However we found a possible risk of interference between the mudguard mounting bracket and the brake cable. On the prototype there is ~1mm of clearance, but if the welding tolerance is slightly off (fork side bracket is welded closer to the wheel axle), the brake cable will rub on the mudguard fixation nut:

They sent a Chinese datasheet, from what it seems the lock works similarly like the Cobra battery lock. No data communication, simple +5V is needed to operate it. 

*Chatgpt translation:*

h3. _3. Working Principle_

h4. _3.1 Interface Definition_

||_No._||_Wire Color_||_Function_||
|_1_|_Red_|_Power + (VCC)_|
|_2_|_Black_|_Power - (GND)_|
|_3_|_Yellow_|_Unlock Signal Input (High-Level Trigger)_|
|_4_|_Green_|_Lock Status Signal Output (Closed = Low, Open = High)_|

----

h4. _3.2 Working Principle_

_The lock operates with a_ *_motor-driven mechanism_*_. When the controller sends a_ *_high-level unlock signal_*_, the motor rotates, and the_ *_lock tongue retracts_*_, unlocking the mechanism. After the helmet is returned, the lock tongue_ *_automatically extends_*_, and the_ *_position detection switch_* _changes to_ *_closed-circuit (conducting) status_*_, signaling the system that the helmet is secured._



[^ST-509基础版规格书.pdf]

{noformat}def generate_exp_df(vmax_store, experiment_store, rng=None, experiment_measurement_error=None):

    if experiment_store == []:
        experiment_store = [{"channel": "cost_platform_channel", 'cost_before': 0, 'cost_after': 0, 'delta': 0, 'sigma': 0}]

    else:
        exp_df = pd.DataFrame(experiment_store)
        exp_df['vmax'] = exp_df['channel'].map(vmax_store)
    
        exp_df['delta_from_curve'] = exp_df.apply(
        lambda row: abs(mm_saturation(row['cost_before'], row['vmax'], row['vmax']) - mm_saturation(row['cost_after'], row['vmax'], row['vmax']) ), axis=1)

        # Introducing measurement error here (Uniform):
        exp_df['delta'] = exp_df.apply(lambda row: max(0,row['delta_from_curve'] +

Hey [~accountid:5fa01e19aea468006a8a298e] 

They’ve included two proposed clauses:

{quote}(1) “The accumulated and aggregate liabilities of the Receiving Party under or in connection with this Agreement shall not exceed the total value of the Project Contract related to this Agreement.”{quote}

{quote}(2) “Notwithstanding any other provision of this Agreement, a Party shall not be liable to the other Party for loss of revenues or profits, loss of goodwill or any indirect, incidental, or consequential loss or damages in connection with the performance or non-performance of this Agreement.”{quote}

Neither are appropriate for the document for the following reasons:

* The “Project Contract” is not yet in place and in any event referring to its value as a liability cap introduces unnecessary ambiguity.
* The NDA does not create financial obligations or performance duties, so excluding liability for indirect/consequential loss is disproportionate and misaligned with the agreement’s limited scope.
* The standard NDA already limits liability implicitly by restricting use and requiring return of information, with no commitments beyond confidentiality and good faith handling.

Suggest they sign the NDA as is and we can discuss liability caps/consequential losses in the actual project contract - the appropriate place for these provisions.

+*BACKGROUND*+

* Bolt is entering into an agreement with YunoJuno. The latter is providing staff services under a Global Services Agreement.
** YunoJuno’s services include identifying, onboarding, managing, and processing payments for freelance talent (i.e., delivery oversight and resource continuity) in Europe and Africa. In other words, YunoJuno will provide and pay freelance staff.
* Factual circumstances of processing (based on the agreement):
** “_Provision of freelance talent sourcing, onboarding, management, and payment services. Includes identity verification, communication, and system access management as required for service delivery_”
** Date being processed: Employee name, contact details, transaction history; customer name, contact details, address and location information. Also possible freelancer payment / banking details.
*** Includes freelancers, Bolt employees and website visitors.
* Gab previously reviewed and noted that the agreement foresees a controller-controller relationship. However, given the nature of services (talent sourcing, onboarding, payments), “_YunoJuno clearly processes personal data on behalf of Bolt and therefore should be categorized as a processor_”.
** Gab provided a pre-filled DPA.

+*UPDATE (28.07)*+

* YunoJuno has pushed back on the characterisation as a processor in [this draft|https://docs.google.com/document/d/1l-H_8R2s8UwpO1VUH8eWQJQ5Q6NL7gnT/edit].

+*THOUGHTS*+

* It sounds like YunoJuno manages the lifecycle of freelancers for Bolt. In a few instances, this would indeed indicate a processor role. But not all.
** Under EDPB 07/2020, payroll administration usually indicates a processor.
** Under EDPB 07/2020, headhunters _can_ be considered joint controllers.
* Ultimately, it is *_fact-dependent_* whether this is as a controller or processor.
** (a) If YunoJuno independently decides which freelancers are matched, how onboarding is done, data retention policies, or uses freelancer data for its own operational decisions (and not strictly under our instructions), this could indicate that they are a controller.
** (b) If, on the other hand, YunoJuno works strictly under our direction—identifying specific freelancers we request, onboarding per our policy, only processing data as agreed - then they are a processor.
* Therefore, it would be helpful to understand more about the data processing at-issue here. This would strengthen any arguments I have when having a call with YunoJuno, as it appears currently that discussions have been had which I have no visibility of.

+*NEXT STEPS*+

* Questions:
** *Who decides* which freelancer to engage and on what basis?
** *Who chooses the methods* for verification, onboarding procedures, data retention, communication tools?
** *Does YunoJuno independently reuse or aggregate freelancer data* for its own purposes (e.g. analytics, marketing, platform development)?
* Depending on the degree of control, either defend the position or relent to controllership.

Hello!

Thank you for reaching out!

You are correct, Estonian law states 28 calendar days annual leave. 

Annual leave in Workday is based on 20 working days. Annual leave in payroll program is based on 28 calendar days (it includes all weekdays with weekend days), as it is by Estonian legislation. WD does not deduct weekend days.

There are two ways possible to calculate holiday pay - on the basis of the average salary or by maintaining monthly salary. Our payroll system is set up to choose the more beneficial calculation. Usually the calculation with maintaining monthly salary is more beneficial to the employees. For example your June vacation compensation is also calculated with maintaining monthly salary. 

All final payments are calculated based on 28 calendar days, taking into consideration that 28 calendar days (weekends included) = 4 weeks = 20 working days.

Kind regards
Keidi

Summary:

* our alerting and unotis components try their best to deliver the message to the team
* there is one scenario though when delivery fails, and we do not receive an alert about that:
when unotis fails to deliver and logs
{noformat}node.log_message: "Failed to perform operation, can't retry - out of attempts"{noformat}
In this case, we do not have an alert for that.
* it is unclear what exactly should be changed in unotis to get its state tracked via existing alerting system.
** We do not want to self-DDOS when “Slack fails → unotis fails to deliver → alert for that triggers → unotis fails to deliver → alert for that triggers → …”.
** Some scenarios are OK and should not be acted upon - when delivery failed to people with “@bolt-outsource.eu” emails.
** Some failures are legit like this one:

!image-20250728-143519.png|width=85.52855924978687%,alt="image-20250728-143519.png"!
There were no team detected for a service (service was recently created, and I guess some caches didn’t receive info about that yet).
** etc.

Thus, I mark this ticket as “RnD” - to understand what exactly should be done to bring a proper visibility into unotis' internals in a nice way with a proper quality.


----

Elaboration.

This ticket was created due to PINT gov crew receiving alerts like these:

!image-20250728-133949.png|width=1353,height=884,alt="image-20250728-133949.png"!

Why these alerts were coming to this channel?

* there are secrets for packages which do not exists anymore. Secrets for these packages are owned by pint gov crew by default:
{noformat}src/foundation/backend/backend_credentials/main/config/config.defaults.production.ts:74{noformat}
* when package gets deleted, and 1 year passes since creation of a secret => alert for “obsolete secret” shall be sent to the owner which is PINT gov crew
* but PINT gov crew does not have an alerting channel, only support.
* If there is no alerting channel for a team, the corresponding message will be sent to the team’s support channel. That’s exactly the messages shown on a screenshot: PINT gov crew team does not have an alerting channel, only support, and message tells about that.



With that: since PINT gov crew does not own any services at the moment, we can safely ignore getting “obsolete secrets” alerts for services owned by PINT gov crew because these packages/services do not exist anymore. I updated alerting rule [https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/backend-alerting/rules/edit/91413?tab=rules|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/backend-alerting/rules/edit/91413?tab=rules] to reflect that.

----

Now, what will happen if team does not have an alerting channel set?

# Here
{noformat}src/foundation/monitoring/alerting_forwarder/main/service/Forwarder.ts:235{noformat}
alerting will try to get code owner or service ID, and if there is some - it will tell {{unotis}} to send message to the team’s channel.
# If team cannot be found, it will increase counter, and “unmatched alert” for PINT will trigger according to this rule: [https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/backend-alerting/rules/edit/31?tab=details|https://admin-panel.bolt.eu/backend-alerting/rules/edit/31?tab=details]
# If team was found, unotis tries its best to find at least some Slack channel belonging to the team:
{noformat}src/foundation/backend/unotis/main/service/messageSender/SlackDeliverySystem.ts:251{noformat}
# If unotis fails hard after retrying, it logs error to Kibana:
{noformat}src/foundation/backend/unotis/main/service/messageSender/SlackDeliverySystem.ts:302{noformat}
Currently, there is no alerts for these kind of failures when unotis couldn’t deliver a message.

Internal: discussion is ongoing in Slack. Currently, pending point is liability - the customer lead is ready to proceed with all Bolt changes if Bolt accept an updated liability clause. 

*Advice to the business re/ the liability clause:*

Currently the clause reads that Bolt would be fully liable and must reimburse the customer for any data protection-related fines, even if its not Bolt's fault - which is high risk. *Real-life scenario:* if the customer mismanages access to the Bolt Business account and leaks credentials which causes a data breach, Bolt could still be forced to pay for resulting fines or claims, despite not being at [fault.To|http://fault.To] balance this out, I would *at least* suggest the following small update (in bold):

{quote}_Bolt would be liable in full and would be obliged to reimburse for any costs incurred by the Client, in particular the reimbursement of the amount of compensation, damages or a fine, if the Client is obliged by a final decision or a final judgement of a competent court to pay a fine, damages, or any other amount for a breach of personal data protection regulations,_ *_to the extent such obligation arises due to Bolt’s own breach of applicable data protection laws_*_._{quote}

*Additionally, as a good to have, I would suggest the following:*

# Some liability cap to protect us - if the customer does not accept the standard of 3 months worth of fees, I would suggest 12 months as an industry-standard alternative - but the cap is a business decision. My general advice is to limit the cap as much as possible, as GDPR fines in Poland can reach beyond 1 million EUR, and on EU level, GDPR fines can be up to 4% of annual turnover. However - with our processing operations in Bolt Business, if something goes wrong, its unlikely in my view for the business customer to receive any substantial fines due to Bolt's fault - *so I assess the risk as low if we proceed without a cap.*
# Make the clause mutual, so Bolt is similarly protected against breaches by the customer. This is not critical because the customer gets very limited amount of Bolt's data, and  because of this, any breach on their end is very unlikely to get escalated.

Ticket Resoluton:

”The retention of courier deposit amounts as described by you *should not be considered reportable under DAC7,* neither as consideration received by the Seller nor as a platform fee, i.e. the courier is not receiving any compensation and the retained amount does not qualify as a fee associated with the platform’s facilitation of relevant activities.

Further explanation is below.

_____________________________________

*Consideration* means compensation in any form that is paid or credited to a reportable seller (e.g. courier) in connection with a relevant activity (e.g delivery).

In our case:

* The courier is not being paid or credited any amount - they are forfeiting a previously refundable deposit (i.e. they don’t receive anything, in fact they lose the right for a refund).
* The retained deposit is not directly linked to the provision of a relevant activity - it’s an incidental policy around equipment usage, not a core platform-mediated activity.

*Platform fee* in the DAC7 context typically refers to:

* A charge imposed by the platform for facilitating a relevant activity (e.g. delivery);
* An amount deducted from the seller’s earnings (e.g. commissions, service charges);
* Directly linked to access, usage, or monetisation of platform services.

In our case, the deposit:

* Was paid upfront and not deducted from earnings;
* Wasn’t charged in exchange for access or facilitation of platform services.
* Was refundable, reinforcing its treatment as a security deposit, not a charge;
* The retention stems from a contractual forfeiture after a non-return, not from the facilitation of a delivery service.”

{panel:bgColor=#ffebe6}
*Mexico*

* The use of facial biometrics (selfie verification) in Mexico triggers compliance requirements under the 2025 LFPDPPP.
* Biometric data is classified as _sensitive personal data_ and requires *express written consent* (e.g. electronic signature). Our current bundled consent mechanism (“Confirm” button with “by continuing” language) is unlikely to meet this standard.

*Key considerations*:

* *Consent format*: Bundled purposes (e.g. ID verification + fraud prevention) and lack of specificity weaken consent validity.
* *Cross-border transfers*: Require express consent or a valid legal exemption.
* *Enforcement risk*: Active authority; fines for sensitive data breaches can be *doubled*—up to *MXN 32 million (~€1.7M)*.
* *Criminal exposure*: Serious violations (e.g. deceptive processing) may trigger *3 months–3 years’ imprisonment* for individuals.

{{Recommendation: Refrain from launch unless consent flows are redesigned and validated locally.}}
{panel}

{panel:bgColor=#ffebe6}
*Zambia*

* Zambia’s Data Protection Act (2021) prohibits processing of sensitive personal data, including biometrics, *unless a specific legal exemption applies*. *Consent is not a valid basis* under this framework.
* While passed in 2021, the Act became enforceable only in *2023* with the establishment of the *Data Protection Commission (DPC)*. Since *March 2025*, the regulator has initiated active enforcement—registration mandates, audits, and compliance notices.

*Key considerations*:

* *No applicable exemption*: Bolt’s use case doesn’t meet legal claim, or medical exceptions. There is a potential argument to rely on 'public interest' exemption, but the likelihood of it being successful is very low.
* *Consent insufficient*: Explicit opt-in does not make biometric processing lawful.
* *Penalties*:
** Companies: *Up to 2% of global turnover* or *ZMW 600,000*.
** Individuals: *Up to ZMW 300,000* or *10 years’ imprisonment*.
* *Registration required*: Mandatory for all data controllers; unregistered processing is a criminal offence.
* *Other obligations*: DPIA, data localisation or approved transfer mechanisms required.

{{Recommendation: Do not proceed with launch  without a special authorisation from the regulator - not guaranteed}} 
{panel}

In our opinion, *the passport of a Ukrainian citizen whose validity has been extended by the Ukrainian consulate in Poland with the appropriate stamp in the passport is valid and should be treated as a sufficient identity document.*

The possibility of extending the validity of the passport of a Ukrainian citizen by the consulate of Ukraine was introduced on the basis of Resolution No. 170 of the Council of Ministers of Ukraine of February 28, 2022 "On certain issues regarding the entry of information into the passport of a Ukrainian citizen for travel abroad", which assumes that *the passport can be extended for a period of 5 years only in two situations*:

# when it is not technically possible to issue a new passport (e.g. no access to the demographic register) at the migration office or consulate, or
# when there is a sudden need to urgently go abroad due to outgoing treatment, accompanying a seriously ill person or the death of a loved one abroad.

In such cases, the consul *extends the validity of the passport* by entering an appropriate annotation/stamp in the passport. Such a stamp of the embassy/consulate changes the *status of the document* – the passport is no longer treated as "expired", but as *extended and still valid*, so it can be legally used to verify identity in the territory of the Republic of Poland until the newly indicated expiry date.

In practice, many consulates have gradually restored *the full technical capacity to issue new passports*, so *extending a passport is treated as an exceptional measure*. However, *consulates still extend the validity of passports in justified cases*, which is confirmed by official consular instructions (for example, Ukrainian embassies in various countries inform about the possibility of extending the validity of the document for people whose passports are expiring if they cannot obtain a new passport immediately).

From 23 April 2024, all Ukrainian consulates *have stopped providing services to men of military age*. From this date, men of military age will only be able to apply for *documents that allow them to return to Ukraine, i.e. the so-called "white passport".*

This means that men between the ages of 18 and 60 whose passports have expired *will not be able to obtain a new passport at the consulate*.

The Polish National Labour Inspectorate (PIP) has published information on the expiry of the passports of Ukrainian citizens and their continued ability to work in Polish. In the opinion of the PIP, *the expiry of the passport of a Ukrainian citizen does not affect* the legal situation of the foreigner *in terms of the legality of his/her work.*
